memos.title: The substrate chokepoint that already re-rated
memos.dek: AXT owns roughly 40% of the indium-phosphide substrate supply the entire laser chain grows on — but the venture-scale move already happened, and the desk is on watch, not chase.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $AXTI (AXT Inc) manufactures compound-semiconductor substrates — the indium-phosphide (InP) and gallium-arsenide wafers that photonics lasers are physically grown on. In the analyst's framing it controls roughly **40% of the InP substrate supply chain**, sitting one layer upstream of every laser maker in the [[photonics]] story, from [[sive]] to [[lite]].

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
Every CW laser, EML and epiwafer in the optical ramp starts life on an InP substrate, and supply is concentrated in a handful of names. The confirmed anchor: a 3-year wafer supply deal with Coherent ([[cohr]]), including a **$22,288,500 prepayment** to AXT-Tongmei for committed capacity (8-K, 25 Jun). Around it, a Nomura report he relayed cites 2-inch InP substrate price hikes of 42-76%, 3-inch hikes of ~78%, and 50-75% on EML epiwafers — the [[chokepoint]] pattern this desk tracks across the map.

The desk's caution is about what's already in the price, not the mechanism: part of the ASP spike is a China export-control artifact (licenses began flowing in June 2026, and AXT is doubling capacity), so the hikes can normalize rather than compound.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: It is the purest upstream expression of the optical build-out: if transceiver and CPO volumes ramp the way the [[photonics]] names require, substrate demand rises with all of them regardless of which laser vendor wins. The Coherent prepayment is exactly what a real chokepoint looks like — customers paying eight figures up front for committed capacity.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: The re-rating already happened — his own post describes the stock going 'from $1 to $60' (it peaked well above that), so today's buyer is not getting the trade his original thesis sized. The ASP-spike leg can unwind as export licenses normalize supply. His standing dilution warning applies most sharply here, and this week's three mentions were all list-posts plus a bare 'still holding' — mention-count momentum, not new evidence.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch — the chokepoint is real but the venture-scale move is behind it. Re-engage on a real reset (a 30-40% retrace toward the run's base) with substrate ASPs still rising; the Nomura hike schedule is the dashboard. Chasing list-post momentum after a hundred-bagger leg is how the [[conviction-tier]] system gets people hurt.

memos.title: The washout he asked for arrived — and he bought it
memos.dek: Applied Optoelectronics ran from the analyst's entry to a multi-bagger, crashed 40–60% with the optical complex, and his own framework said that dip was the entry.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $AAOI makes optical transceivers — the modules that convert electrical signals to light so GPU racks can move data at bandwidths copper physically cannot carry. It sits in the [[photonics]] layer as the volume-manufacturing pure play, and it is one of the analyst's two most concentrated holdings alongside $SIVE.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The headline claim is aggressive: a ~$1.4B/quarter revenue run-rate by H1 2027 — 800%+ year-over-year growth — driven by hyperscaler transceiver demand, stated off a market cap that makes the multiple look cheap *if* the ramp is real. The analyst himself called the stock overextended after its huge run and predicted range-bound chop until earnings.

Then the washout came: the SemiAnalysis CPO-delay pieces plus the Bloomberg Meta-compute story knocked optical names down 40–60%. His response was to buy heavily — and notably, the desk's own prior verdict had named exactly this condition ("a washout back toward the pre-run range") as the entry trigger. The condition fired; the stance upgraded from watch to accumulate.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Of the transceiver names, AAOI has the clearest single-story torque: one revenue ramp, one customer concentration question, one earnings print that settles it. The desk's read is that the 40–60% drawdown transferred most of the froth out of the position while the claimed monthly run-rate trajectory — roughly $471M/month at target — remained untested rather than disproven. An AMD CW long-term-agreement relationship gives the story a second leg beyond the hyperscaler transceiver ramp.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The run-rate story is still narrative until an earnings print validates it — 800% growth claims fail more often than they land. The analyst is heavily concentrated and openly suffering drawdowns here, so reiterations carry maximum book-talking risk; the desk discounts frequency and weights only new datapoints. And AAOI is the highest-beta expression of a complex that just demonstrated it can lose half its value on two blog posts.

AAOI is now an explicit sell-side battleground: B. Riley's sell case argues network flattening cuts transceiver TAM 40-50%, while Rosenblatt counters that XPU count grows faster than per-XPU optics shrink, so total optical demand still rises. Expect headline whipsaw into the print.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate — scale in on the washout rather than paying up after the earnings confirmation, but keep half the intended size in reserve for the print. The new sell-report noise is not a thesis change; it raises the stakes on the earnings event that was always the decisive test of the $471m/month run-rate claim.

memos.title: A dated catalyst inside a boring giant
memos.dek: Jabil's 1.6T optical module qualification — Aug 2026 to Mar 2027, then mass production with Sivers lasers — gives the conservative photonics expression an actual clock.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $JBL is a contract electronics giant whose relevance to this map is one program: it builds 1.6T LRO optical modules for AI datacenters, feeding the same interconnect demand as the pure plays in [[photonics]] — with a diversified multi-billion-revenue base underneath instead of a single-product balance sheet.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
This week produced the book's most concrete new datapoint, and it attaches here. Per a JPM fireside chat the analyst relayed, JBL management described a "relatively dramatic moat" in its 1.6T LRO, with qualification completing over the following months — an **Aug 2026 to Mar 2027** window — and mass production starting afterward, using $SIVE lasers in the pluggables. That converts JBL from a vague conservative-expression idea into a thesis with a dated, checkable catalyst.

It also makes JBL the keystone of the analyst's photonics stack: the same qualification event de-risks his SIVE position, which is worth remembering when weighing his enthusiasm.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: It is the low-risk door into the highest-conviction corner of the book. If 1.6T optics ramp, JBL participates with manufacturing scale no pure play can match; if they slip, JBL remains a profitable EMS business and the position costs patience, not capital. The catalyst is verifiable from public sources — qualification completion and optics revenue commentary on the next two earnings calls — so the thesis does not depend on trusting anyone's enthusiasm.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: Dilution of impact is the structural one: optics can succeed and still be too small to move a ~$28B-revenue company's needle — the bull case needs optics broken out or visibly bending the growth rate. Program risk is the sharp one: qualification slipping past Q1 2027 or losing transceiver share to rival EMS suppliers guts the thesis. And note the sourcing: the moat language is management's own, relayed secondhand through the analyst — friendlier telephone than a filed disclosure.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate — the starter position stands, with the qualification window as the concrete thing to verify across the next two earnings calls. Add if optics contribution starts getting broken out or the qual completes on schedule. Slip past Q1 2027 and the desk folds this back to watch.

memos.title: The incumbent way to own the laser bottleneck
memos.dek: Lumentum is the lower-torque, lower-drama expression of the same photonics chokepoint — the anchor holding of the sleeve while SIVE and AXTI carry the risk.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $LITE builds industrial lasers and the optical components inside datacenter transceivers and telecom gear — the incumbent supplier at the [[photonics]] layer where $SIVE is the challenger. In this coverage universe it plays a specific role: the established, revenue-generating way to own the laser bottleneck without underwriting a micro-cap's balance sheet.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The analyst's frame is that laser supply stays bottlenecked **into 2029** — demand from 1.6T pluggables and CPO scale-out compounds faster than laser capacity can be added. His standing heuristic: when the CEO says everything they make gets bought, sell-side bear notes about valuation do not touch the fundamentals. The recent washout gave that frame a live test — LITE fell 4–10% alongside the whole complex on what he reads as cascading margin liquidations plus the SemiAnalysis CPO-delay pieces, none of it name-specific.

A second-order kicker appeared with the Hesai story: US national-security scrutiny of the Chinese lidar maker is bullish for western lidar players, and upstream, for their laser suppliers — LITE and SIVE both.

The week's channel check hardened the supply side of the argument: Chinese laser makers reportedly have no working 200G EMLs and remain far from the high-power CW lasers that CPO needs — meaning the capacity the bears assumed was coming isn't visible yet.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Same chokepoint as the small-caps, a fraction of the fragility. LITE has scale, customer breadth, and actual current earnings against the same structural shortage. In sleeve terms it is the low-beta anchor: if the photonics thesis is right, LITE re-rates with it; if the thesis is early, LITE's drawdowns are survivable in a way SIVE's may not be.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: The bear case that matters is the one SemiAnalysis argued: CPO delays plus hyperscaler order pushouts would hit the growth narrative even if today's business holds. The subtler risk is competitive — LITE currently buys from some of the CW-laser entrants; if names like SIVE graduate from suppliers to rivals on next-gen sockets, the incumbent loses share exactly where the growth was supposed to come from. Note also the evidence quality: this week's citations are washout commentary and a second-order lidar story, not new LITE-specific datapoints.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate — keep building the anchor position on red days and let [[sive]]/[[axti]] carry the torque. Rosenblatt's read that short sellers plan to cover in late July/August suggests the red days are numbered; nothing in the current evidence changes sizing. What would: an actual (not reported-then-denied) CPO slip, or Chinese high-power CW capacity showing up in channel checks.

memos.title: The center of the map is not the trade
memos.dek: NVIDIA is the demand hub every thesis here feeds into — which is precisely why this desk expresses the view through the suppliers, not the hub.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $NVDA is the gravitational center of this entire coverage universe: every name in the book either supplies into its chips, manufactures them, connects them, or builds on top of them. It carries a desk verdict not because it is a pick, but because it is the reference point every other verdict is measured against — see [[accelerators]].

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: The analyst rarely publishes NVDA-specific work, and that is the point. His edge — and this tool's — lives in the layers beneath: the optics, lasers, memory and substrates where a design win moves a small company's entire valuation rather than a mega-cap's next quarter. This week NVDA featured only as collateral: the selloff he attributes to a misleading Bloomberg piece on Meta compute plus SemiAnalysis bear posts on NVDA supply chains, and the Hesai lidar scrutiny in which NVDA is the partner under review.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Not the question this desk answers. The honest framing: if you want NVDA exposure, that is a core-portfolio allocation decision made outside this workflow. What this coverage universe offers instead is the derivative trade — names whose fortunes are levered to NVDA's roadmap at multiples of the payoff and multiples of the risk.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: For this book, NVDA is the risk factor rather than the position: a genuine NVDA demand shock (hyperscaler capex cuts, an export-control expansion, a credible custom-silicon displacement story) hits every supplier here harder than it hits NVDA itself. The narrative war matters too — this week showed that two bearish supply-chain posts can mark the whole complex down 40–60% from the highs, fundamentals untouched.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch. Express the view through the suppliers this map surfaces; hold NVDA as a separate decision. The desk would re-rate this into an active call only if the analyst starts publishing NVDA-specific supply or pricing work — that is the falsifier for keeping it parked.

memos.title: The laser everyone else's thesis depends on
memos.dek: Sivers sells the continuous-wave lasers that JBL, GlobalFoundries, Ayar and POET all need — the analyst's favorite name, and his most concentrated bet.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body:
$SIVE makes indium-phosphide continuous-wave (CW) DFB lasers — the light source that co-packaged optics and next-gen pluggable transceivers cannot work without. It is fab-lite, Sweden-listed, and mapped as the laser supplier into $JBL's 1.6T modules, $GFS's reference design, Ayar Labs' NVLink-attached CPO, and [[photonics]] scale-out plays like $POET.

This is the analyst's highest-conviction name — "probably my favorite stock right now" — and also his largest holding, which is exactly why this memo exists: the desk's job is to separate the supply-chain logic (strong) from the book-talking (structural).

Late-week development: three insider purchases landed right after the drop — most notably the CEO buying 1,000,000 SEK of stock on the open market — while Nvidia denied the delay reports that caused the selloff and a sell-side channel check concluded Chinese rivals are 'quite far' from high-power CW lasers.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The chokepoint argument is simple: everyone building CPO or 1.6T optics needs CW lasers, few suppliers exist, and Sivers sits on qualification tracks at several of them at once. The most dateable claim is the $JBL leg — per a JPM fireside chat the analyst relayed, JBL's 1.6T LRO qualification should complete between **Aug 2026 and Mar 2027**, followed by mass production with Sivers lasers in the pluggables. AEVA targets high-volume manufacturing around Q4 2026 and $POET H2 2026, so the demand waves are staggered rather than simultaneous.

On top sit the corporate catalysts he cites: an oversubscribed funding round for the fabless ramp, a NASDAQ listing "in the next few quarters," then M&A for TAM expansion. His valuation hook is relative — it trades below $POET while supplying half the ecosystem POET belongs to.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: If the CPO transition happens at all, the discrete CW laser is one of the few places where a small company owns a genuine bottleneck rather than renting a story. The multi-customer structure matters: this is not a one-design-win bet, it is four or five partially independent qualification tracks, any one of which validates the ramp. The NASDAQ listing is a separate, non-fundamental catalyst — a liquidity re-rate that does not require the technology thesis to resolve first.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Every flag the desk tracks is live here. It is the analyst's largest position, so every reiteration is also an advertisement. The auditor has raised a going-concern flag around the SEK 700M raise, and Ningi Research has published a short thesis — if the cash strain is real, dilution does the damage before any design win pays. Integrated-laser architectures (OpenLight-style, needing no external light source) are the technology kill-shot: they remove the discrete CW supplier from the diagram entirely. And the newest angle — Hesai lidar scrutiny pushing western lidar toward $LITE/$SIVE lasers — is second-order speculation, not orders.

Qualification risk is the dateable one: $JBL slipping past Q1 2027, or a design-out at JBL/GFS/Ayar, breaks the strongest leg of the thesis.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate, on the staggered plan — and this week supplied the tranche trigger the plan was waiting for: a CEO open-market buy into a headline-driven drop, both delay reports denied, and Rosenblatt reporting the short sellers pressuring the sector intend to cover in late July/August. The desk treats that combination as the add-on-dip window. What breaks the thesis is unchanged: insider selling resuming, the NASDAQ listing slipping, or the [[jbl]]/GlobalFoundries partnerships failing to convert to volume orders.

memos.title: Capacity into an upgraded cycle — and a boundary drawn
memos.dek: Innolight revised 800G demand upward the same week AAOI broke ground in Texas; the desk also now knows exactly what this bet is not.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Two things changed since the last memo, one bullish and one clarifying. Bullish: Innolight's investor relations revised **800G transceiver demand sharply upward** ('demand has not contracted; instead, 800G demand has increased significantly'), with new customer types — neoclouds, AI model companies — broadening the base beyond hyperscalers. Clarifying: the analyst's own channel work concedes $AAOI has **no CPO design wins**, with the CEO calling commercial timing 'TBD.' This is a pluggables business, full stop.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: The bet is torque to the 800G/1.6T pluggable cycle, with capacity arriving into demand that was just revised up. AAOI formally commenced its ~400,000 sq ft Texas manufacturing buildout, supported by state and local subsidies, on top of the prior $20.85M package. His $471m/month H2-2027 revenue framing remains the bull anchor; the Innolight revision is the first outside datapoint since the bear report that leans his way. The bull/bear fight (B. Riley's network-flattening sell case versus Rosenblatt's XPU-count counter) is unresolved and makes the earnings print the decisive event.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Among the [[photonics]] names, AAOI is the highest-torque way to own the pluggable demand revision: smaller than $LITE/$COHR, capacity growing into the cycle, and now with a demand datapoint (800G revised up, longer tail) that directly feeds its product mix. The subsidized buildout lowers the capital cost of being wrong on timing.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: The no-CPO clarification is a genuine boundary: if the industry transition to co-packaged optics comes faster than the 800G tail sustains, AAOI is on the wrong side of the architecture with no design-win hedge — the exact scenario where $SIVE/$LITE/$COHR win and pluggable pure-plays lose. It is also now a named battleground stock; expect headline whipsaw into the print, in both directions. Execution risk on a 400k sq ft ramp is real for a company this size.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate, unchanged: hold the scale-in from the washout, keep the reserved half for the earnings print. Treat CPO headlines — good and bad — as noise for AAOI specifically; the variables that matter are 800G/1.6T pluggable volume and the Texas ramp timeline. Back to watch on an earnings miss against the monthly run-rate narrative, or on evidence CPO is cannibalizing pluggables faster than the revised demand supports.

memos.title: A venture bet wearing a ticker
memos.dek: Agility Robotics' SPAC is the analyst's most concentrated robotics conviction — and the desk's clearest case of a real asset inside a dangerous structure.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body:
$CCXI is the SPAC that becomes $AGLT around September — Agility Robotics, the US humanoid maker whose Digit robots are already deployed inside $AMZN and MELI warehouses, with Amazon, $NVDA, SoftBank and Foxconn on the cap table. The analyst ranks it the #1 US humanoid player by commercialization today (ahead of $TSLA Optimus and Figure) and has said outright he's 'trying to own as much % of Agility as possible' — his highest robotics concentration.

The desk covers it because the [[robotics]] theme now has institutional scaffolding — an SVRC 'State of Robotics' report lists Agility second among US national champions, and an IBK value-chain report supplies the tracking framework — but rates it below his conviction, deliberately.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The macro leg is geopolitical: China ships ~90% of the world's humanoid robots, and a US champion is politically and commercially valuable the moment Washington notices. The micro leg is valuation relativity: Agility came public-market-accessible at roughly **$3–4B pre-money** while Figure — a less commercialized, general-purpose competitor — was last valued at **$39B** privately. Add a RoboFab targeting 10K+ units/year with ~75% US-sourced components (against Tesla's China-dependent bill of materials), and a planned deployment path through the warehouse customers it already serves.

Institutions are arriving on schedule: BlueCrest disclosed a 5.6% stake within days of the announcement. The forward indicator the desk tracks, per the IBK framework, is actuator capacity — roughly 310K actuators per 10K robots — which reads on the whole theme's ramp, not just Agility's.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: It is the only public, pure-play access to a US humanoid program at a valuation still anchored near its private round — the exact retail-access structure the analyst praises Unitree for. If the S-curve he sketches (his 2030 guess: 90–140K units industry-wide versus institutions modeling ~30K) is even directionally right, the commercialized player inside Amazon's deployment machine is positioned to take the volume before the general-purpose labs ship anything.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: Start with the messenger: this is maximum talking-his-book territory — he owns it heavily, says so, and posts about it constantly, so the mention count badly overstates independent signal. Then the structure: it is still a SPAC, and his own critique of $BOT (trading at 3.5x its published NAV) applies uncomfortably well to any de-SPAC riding theme euphoria — dilution at the ticker change, a float that hasn't settled, and a market he himself describes as an 'ADHD goldfish' rotating through hot themes. Finally the industry: China's price war in humanoids can crush unit economics before US production scales.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch — not because the asset is fake, but because the structure and the euphoria phase price it as if execution were done. If it must be owned, size it as venture risk: small, no adds on spikes, and let the post-SPAC float settle first. Upgrades on a funded, dated Amazon deployment contract or a US robotics subsidy program; downgrades on dilution at the $AGLT conversion or the SPAC closing below the cited valuation. The desk's fuller theme view lives in [[robotics]].

memos.title: The memory leader the desk won't chase
memos.dek: Micron has the cycle, the contracts and the scale — which is exactly why the marginal upside lives elsewhere in the memory book.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $MU is the US memory flagship — DRAM, HBM and NAND — and the name the market reaches for first when the [[memory]] theme works. The analyst treats every MU dip as a buying opportunity and cites his gross-margin model being 'validated ahead of time' as DRAM/NAND hikes landed. The desk added this verdict at operator request, and rates it below his enthusiasm on purpose.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The demand case is contract-hardened: **16+ long-term agreements** signed, plus a new LTA with $QCOM announced this week — and the stock fell 5%+ on that news, which he reads as the tail end of margin-cascade deleveraging rather than anything fundamental. Pricing momentum is verified from multiple directions: UBS models DDR contract prices **+32% in Q3 and +18% in Q4** (above prior estimates) with NAND +30%; Samsung is seeking 20% DRAM hikes; TrendForce sees server DRAM up 13–18%. On the supply side MU is leading a ~¥1.5 trillion investment in Hiroshima — capex into a cycle it has pre-sold.

His rotation frame says memory and photonics alternate as the market's favorite bottleneck, with memory 'bottlenecked into 2029.' Nothing this week contradicts that.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: It is the broadest, lowest-idiosyncratic-risk expression of the memory upcycle: US-listed, mega-cap, diversified across DRAM, HBM and NAND, with demand visibility that smaller players can't match. If the upcycle is real and you want one memory name you never have to babysit, this is the candidate.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: The desk's reservation is about upside capture, not safety. Micron retained **price ceilings and floors** in its strategic customer agreements — while SK Hynix reportedly scrapped its caps — so the flagship participates less in the spot-price spike than the headline hikes suggest. Scale cuts the same way: on the sharpest sub-cycles the analyst himself points at Winbond, Macronix and SkyHigh as the cleaner beneficiaries because MU's ~$1T market position dwarfs the affected TAM. And his MU conviction is his weakest form of signal — dip-buy remarks and list-post appearances, never a dedicated deep dive with numbers.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch. The desk's memory torque is already expressed through $SNDK, where the NAND repricing bites hardest and the market's disbelief is deepest; MU is the consensus way in, and consensus is priced. Upgrades on evidence its LTA terms participate in spot upside, or a dedicated MU thesis from the analyst. If DRAM contract momentum breaks, the whole memory book downgrades — SNDK first, this name second.

memos.title: The purest neocloud, graded by its customers
memos.dek: Nebius keeps winning exactly the contracts its thesis predicted — the desk's job now is grading the counterparties signing them.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $NBIS is the analyst's highest-conviction [[neoclouds]] name and one of his oldest calls in this corpus — 'the purest Neocloud with execution certainty,' flagged as a potential next hyperscaler back when that was contrarian. The thesis has been repeatedly market-validated since: hyperscaler compute scarcity keeps forcing the giants to rent, and Nebius keeps signing them.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The engine is structural compute scarcity at the top of the stack. The clarifying episode: $GOOGL restricted $META's cloud capacity in March 2026 because Google itself was compute-constrained — its cloud backlog nearly doubled in a quarter — which forced Meta into **$48B+ take-or-pay contracts** with neoclouds including Nebius. When hyperscalers can't rely on each other, the independent GPU cloud is the release valve.

The latest proof is diversification beyond hyperscalers: a **$1B+ agreement with Reflection AI** for GB300 access through 2029. And when the market read Meta's excess-compute-sales plan as neocloud-negative, Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley read it the analyst's way — as validation of underlying AI demand, with take-or-pay contracts insulating the existing base.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: It is the most direct listed expression of the gap between AI compute demand and hyperscaler capacity — with revenue locked in take-or-pay form rather than spot pricing. The customer mix is broadening on schedule: hyperscalers, then AI labs, then enterprises, each signing multi-year commitments. Every capex raise at $META or $MSFT tightens the scarcity that fills Nebius's order book.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: Counterparty quality is now the live one, and the analyst flags it himself: Reflection AI signed multi-billion commitments across several providers and 'might not have the funds to actually execute on these LTAs' — the OpenAI-commitment pattern in miniature. Second, Meta selling excess compute makes a hyperscaler a *competitor* for marginal neocloud demand, which is a structural threat to pricing power even if existing contracts are safe. Third, the model is financing-heavy and contract-concentrated; a debt raise on worse terms changes the risk math faster than the narrative will admit.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate — but grade every new contract by who signed it. Fundable counterparties (hyperscalers, funded enterprises) repricing committed capacity are add signals; model-lab paper commitments are headline risk wearing a press release. What sends this to watch: hyperscaler capex cuts, Meta's resold compute visibly undercutting neocloud pricing, or a major counterparty failing to fund its commitments.

memos.title: The trio is now official
memos.dek: Morgan Stanley put Sivers beside Lumentum and Coherent as the CPO laser leaders — the anonymity discount the accumulation plan harvests has started expiring.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: The week the sell side caught up: Morgan Stanley's CPO note names $SIVE alongside $LITE and $COHR as the laser-supply leaders — a ~$1.5B Swedish-listed company placed next to two $60B+ incumbents, which is the institutional validation of the three-leader framing the analyst built from his own OSINT months ago. The field simultaneously narrowed: MACOM has fallen off the CPO laser map and $AAOI concedes no CPO design wins, so the trio is not just named, it's shrinking toward itself.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
Unchanged in structure, stronger in evidence. The multi-track qualification web — $GFS reference laser, Ayar Labs in the $NVDA NVLink CPO scale-up, $POET scale-out, $JBL 1.6T pluggables, O-Net for ELS mass production — means four or five partially independent paths to volume, any one of which validates the ramp, on his cited ~60% gross margins with Win Semi as manufacturing partner. Demand context hardened too: Innolight's rising silicon-photonics mix shifts industry demand from EML toward exactly the CW lasers Sivers makes, and the sold-out-into-2029 environment at LITE/COHR is now triple-sourced.

His market-structure point — algos miss a name on 'some random Swedish exchange' and it catches up in bursts — is the accumulation window itself, and the MS naming is the beginning of its end.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Still the same asymmetric structure: a genuine bottleneck owned by a small company, multiple independent qualification tracks, and a non-fundamental catalyst (the NASDAQ listing) that re-rates liquidity without needing the technology thesis to resolve first. What's new is that institutional discovery has visibly begun — which raises the odds the re-rate happens before the volume numbers force it.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: Every flag from the first memo stays live, and they are serious: the auditor's going-concern language around the SEK 700M raise, the Ningi short report, dilution risk if cash strain is real, and the integrated-laser (OpenLight-style) architecture kill-shot that removes discrete CW suppliers from the diagram entirely. The messenger risk is maximal — he holds a million-plus shares and says so; at 80+ mentions, this corpus is as much advocacy as analysis. Sell-side validation cuts both ways: institutional attention also means institutional scrutiny of the balance sheet.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate on the staggered plan, unchanged — but the clock is now visible. The ignored-listing discount closes as coverage arrives, so the plan's remaining tranches want red days taken when offered rather than waited for, and the position wants to be built before the NASDAQ listing event. Kill-switches unchanged: insider selling resuming, the listing slipping without explanation, the [[jbl]]/GlobalFoundries tracks failing to convert, or SIVE losing its slot in the trio the sell side just defined.

memos.title: The memory trade the market refuses to believe
memos.dek: SanDisk's Meta supply deal and a verified NAND price upcycle landed the same week memory stocks sold off — the desk opens coverage on the gap.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body:
$SNDK is the NAND flash pure play spun out of Western Digital — one of a handful of companies worldwide that manufacture the flash memory AI datacenters are suddenly consuming at scale. It enters desk coverage this week because the [[memory]] repricing stopped being a narrative and became contracts: a long-term supply agreement with $META confirmed, sector-wide price hikes verified by third-party researchers, and a completed wafer-level burn-in benchmark at $AEHR with a "global leader in NAND flash" that [[aleabitoreddit]] reads as SanDisk.

Unusually for this book, the analyst has never written a dedicated SanDisk thesis — the name surfaces only inside his memory-macro posts. Coverage here rests on the mosaic, and the memo says so plainly.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The claim is that AI inference demand has structurally repriced memory, and NAND is the least-believed leg of it. The analyst's recap cites a **5x general NAND flash price move this year** triggered by RAG and inference workloads, with Samsung and SK Hynix making emergency fab investments to chase it; TrendForce sees server DRAM contracts up 13–18% next quarter with Samsung asking 20%, and SLC NAND forecast up 120–170% into H2. Demand visibility is the new part: $MU has signed 16+ long-term agreements and $META contracted with SanDisk directly — hyperscalers are locking supply years out, which is what turns a price spike into a cycle.

His sharpest observation is the market's reaction: hikes confirmed, LTAs signed — and memory names sold off anyway. The desk agrees that gap is the trade, with one caveat he doesn't make: LTAs cut both ways, capping the seller's price capture as well as guaranteeing volume. Micron kept price ceilings in its agreements; SanDisk's terms are undisclosed.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: It is the purest listed NAND exposure to a repricing that now has contract-backed demand visibility rather than spot-market hope. The $AEHR angle adds free optionality: a completed burn-in benchmark and a potential development agreement around HBF — high-bandwidth flash entering AI inference stacks — would put SanDisk inside the AI bill of materials, not just adjacent to it. And unlike the DRAM majors, a NAND pure play doesn't dilute the cycle across HBM, logic, and foundry exposure.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: Three real ones. First, the mosaic problem: no dedicated thesis from the analyst means no falsifiable single claim to track — this coverage leans on third-party price data more than his work. Second, LTA terms: if SanDisk's agreements cap pricing well below spot, the upcycle accrues to the spot-heavy players instead. Third, the supply response: Samsung and SK Hynix emergency NAND capex is exactly how memory cycles die — if that capacity lands into 2027 demand that has normalized, the cycle inverts fast. The analyst himself flagged the stock approaching $2,000 with shorts wiped out — the run has already happened once, and post-run volatility in this name is violent.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate — but entry discipline is most of the position. Starter tranche into the current memory weakness only, sized small; no chasing green days. Add if the $AEHR HBF development agreement is confirmed as SanDisk or if LTA pricing terms turn out to reset with spot. What sends this back to watch: the 2027 NAND capex wave arriving into softening demand, or the LTA terms revealing capped upside. The desk's fuller reasoning sits in the [[memory]] theme note and the verdict on the watchlist.

memos.title: The run-rate math goes on record
memos.dek: Company-guided $471M/month from H2 2027 against today's market cap is the whole bet — stated plainly during a 50% drawdown.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Crash week made the valuation argument explicit: he calls $AAOI (with $SIVE) 'extremely stupid' cheap, anchored on the company's own $471M/month revenue estimate starting H2 2027 — roughly $5.6B annualized against what he cites as an $8B market cap — while Innolight's sharp 800G upward revision argues that guide gets raised, not cut. The stock dropped ~50% in the crash, then snapped back 15.6% in the recovery.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: A pluggables-cycle bet with capacity arriving into revised-up demand: Texas buildout commenced, 800G demand revised 'more significantly than expected' at Innolight, and the AMD CW LTA relationship in place. Explicitly not a CPO play — his own channel work concedes no CPO design wins — so CPO headlines in either direction are noise for this name.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: If the company guide is even directionally right, the multiple compresses violently. The 800G revision cycle at the bellwether is the first external datapoint suggesting the demand side of that guide is real. Beta cuts both ways but the snap-back showed where the marginal buyer is.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: The entire bet rests on a company projection two years out that has not yet appeared in any quarterly print — his own framing ('is it over if the ramp hasn't shown up when it's 2026?') is honest about that. The B. Riley bear case, margin pressure on pluggables, and the possibility CPO cannibalizes the product line faster than expected all stay live.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate, reserved half still waiting for the earnings print. Crash tranches taken on plan stand; no chasing the recovery. The decisive events are quarterly prints against the run-rate narrative — everything else is commentary.

memos.title: A thermometer, not a thesis
memos.dek: Intel enters coverage on mention volume — but what the corpus actually contains is a memory-cycle quote and a market-bottom gauge, not an Intel idea.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $INTC enters the verdict roster on tier math: crash-week mention volume pushed it into the top 15 by priority score. Honest accounting up front — none of those mentions argue Intel is mispriced. They use Intel: the CEO's 'no relief in memory supply or pricing until at least 2028' as evidence in the memory-shortage case, and 'INTC to LITE' as the span of his market-bottom call.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: There is no Intel thesis in this corpus. What exists is Intel-as-instrument: a senior industry voice on memory scarcity (which supports the $MU/$SNDK book), and a liquid, beaten-down large cap whose behavior marks where the semis bottom is. That's genuinely useful — as a thermometer.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Not established here. A real Intel position is a turnaround judgment on foundry execution, products, and politics — none of which this analyst covers. If you want that bet, it needs a different research base.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: The main risk is category error: reading tier-math entry as a buy signal. The priority score measures attention, and crash weeks generate attention indiscriminately — the focus-weighting catches list-post inflation but can't distinguish 'mentioned as evidence' from 'mentioned as idea'.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch, explicitly as a context name — same treatment as $GOOGL got before it rotated off the roster. Upgrade trigger: a dedicated INTC thesis with numbers (foundry wins, advanced-packaging exposure, CPO-adjacent capacity). Absent that, expect this name to rotate off when the crash-week mentions decay.

memos.title: Goldman marks the sold-out thesis to market
memos.dek: Innolight's estimates raised 65–119% through 2028 on silicon-photonics volumes — the read-through the LITE position was built on, delivered during a liquidation-driven selloff.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: The sold-out-into-2029 thesis got its strongest third-party mark: Goldman Sachs raised Innolight's price target ~164% above market and — more importantly — revised its 2026/2027/2028 earnings estimates up 65%/108%/119%, on much higher silicon-photonics module volumes, 1.6T/3.2T ASP lift, and rising AI capex. He treats Innolight as the $TSM-style read on the whole optical landscape.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Unchanged and now triple-confirmed: the laser giants are sold out for two years and likely into 2029, 800G demand is 'growing more significantly than expected' per Innolight's own transcript, and higher silicon-photonics penetration expands the TAM for every layer beneath the module makers. His historical template is $LITE itself — $3B to $60B+ in two years on the EML chokepoint, before the ~$154B 2028 TAM Goldman now models.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The lower-beta anchor of the photonics book: biggest balance sheet in the trio, sold-out capacity, and the estimate-revision cycle just turned sharply positive at the sector bellwether. The crash proved the demand story survives a liquidity event intact — nothing fundamental broke while the price fell.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: A ~30% drawdown in a month shows the beta even in the 'safe' name. The CPO-delay narrative did real price damage before being refuted, and can again. Concentration risk in hyperscaler order books remains; so does the possibility that CW-laser entrants LITE currently buys from become margin competitors.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate on red days, unchanged. The week's evidence — estimates up at the bellwether while prices went down on liquidations — is the exact configuration the entry discipline was designed for. Kill-switches: hyperscaler pushouts substantiating the CPO-delay bear case, or the revision cycle rolling back over.

memos.title: The buildout starts paying rent
memos.dek: Meta's capex was the bull case for everyone else's revenue — now the $10B Anthropic lease talks make it a revenue line of its own.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: First dedicated memo for the desk's hyperscaler anchor. The event: $META is in talks to lease compute to Anthropic in a $10B deal — the analyst's read is that Meta saw how profitable the SpaceX $45B compute arrangement proved and wants the same trade. A hyperscaler renting out its buildout converts capex critics called a bubble into a rental business with a market price.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Meta functions as the demand-side underwriter of this entire desk: Iris silicon in mass production via AVGO/TSMC with compute doubling to 14GW by 2027, confirmed memory LTAs with $SNDK alongside Micron's agreement book, and hyperscaler capex plans running at the high end of projections. Every leg of the book — photonics, memory, neoclouds — depends on Meta-class capex being real and sustained. The Anthropic talks add a new wrinkle: the buildout monetizes directly, which both validates the neocloud model and makes Meta a future competitor to it.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The lowest-risk expression of the AI-infrastructure demand thesis this corpus is built on. If the buildout thesis is right, Meta wins twice — through its own AI products and now through renting surplus compute. If capex gets cut, this position is the early-warning system for everything else on the desk.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: A guided capex cut is the kill-shot for the whole map, not just this name. The 'agents haven't accelerated' concession could harden into slower buildout. Compute-lease economics are unproven at Meta — talks are talks. And the position is a whole-company bet carrying ad-cycle and regulatory risk this corpus says nothing about.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate on weakness, sized as the book's anchor rather than its alpha. The things to verify: the Anthropic lease closing, Iris hitting September mass production, and capex guidance holding at the high end. Any of those breaking is information about every other position here.

memos.title: Fulfillment falls to 60% — and the desk still watches
memos.dek: Meritz's shortage math and a fresh QCOM LTA harden the memory cycle; the reasons to express it elsewhere harden too.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: The shortage quantified: Meritz Securities (captured at high conviction) argues suppliers can fulfill only 75–80% of DRAM demand in H2 2026, falling to the 60% range in 2027, with SK Hynix at 3.5x and Samsung at 3.9x 2027 P/E on market forecasts. Intel's CEO adds 'no relief in memory supply or pricing until at least 2028'. $MU signed a new LTA with $QCOM on top of its 16+ agreements — and fell 5% on the day.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Memory demand is structural and contracted, and the selloff was deleveraging, not fundamentals — on that, desk and analyst agree. The disagreement stays where it was: whether the flagship captures it. Micron retained price ceilings and floors in its strategic agreements, and his own SLC NAND work shows the sharpest sub-cycles accruing to smaller players (Winbond, Macronix) because MU's scale dwarfs those TAMs.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The lowest-risk direct expression of a shortage that now has sell-side math attached. If LTA terms turn out to participate in spot upside, the ceiling argument dies and the stance upgrades.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: LTA price ceilings capping the upcycle's translation into earnings; crowded ownership; and the cycle risk that emergency capex converts into 2027 oversupply exactly when fulfillment was supposed to bottom.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch, unchanged — the desk's memory torque runs through $SNDK. The falsifier that flips this: LTA terms shown to reset with spot, or a dedicated MU thesis with numbers from him. Until then, treat MU as the cycle's thermometer, not the trade.

memos.title: Nvidia signs the register
memos.dek: A 9.3% NVDA stake goes on the record and Meta starts renting compute like a neocloud — validation from above, with a competitive sting in the tail.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Two headlines in one week: $NVDA disclosed 9.3% beneficial ownership of Nebius via SEC filing (existing 1.19M shares plus a ~21M-share prefunded warrant — not new money, but now official), and $META entered talks to lease $10B of compute to Anthropic, following the template of the SpaceX compute deal. $NBIS rose 17.3% in the recovery day after lagging the initial bounce.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Customer diversification plus committed capacity, now with the industry's most important balance sheet visibly aligned. The Meta-Anthropic talks cut both ways: he reads hyperscalers copying the neocloud model as validation of the business model — the desk agrees, while noting a hyperscaler reselling compute is also tomorrow's competitor with cheaper capital.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The neocloud leader by his framing, with NVDA now a disclosed anchor shareholder, GB300-class committed capacity, and a contract book that grows through both AI-lab and enterprise demand. Sector catalysts (Kimi compute shortage, peer contract wins at IREN and HUT) keep confirming demand exceeds supply.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: Contract quality over contract count: the Reflection AI counterparty caution stands — multi-billion LTAs from model labs that may not be able to fund them. Hyperscaler resale undercutting neocloud pricing is now a live scenario, not a hypothetical. Leverage and capex intensity remain the structural risks of the model.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate, unchanged — but weight adds toward funded counterparties, and treat the NVDA stake as sentiment rather than cash flow. Kill-switches: hyperscaler capex cuts, Meta materially undercutting neocloud pricing, or a major LTA counterparty failing to fund.

memos.title: Denied, recovered, and quietly rearranging the board
memos.dek: Vera Rubin panic closed as predicted; meanwhile NVDA disclosed its Nebius stake and watched AMD copy its Anthropic playbook.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: The delay-rumor cycle resolved exactly as the analyst called it: Jensen's flat Tokyo denial ('Vera Rubin is already in production') held, and the supplier stocks the rumor damaged snapped back in a historic single-day recovery. NVDA itself then moved the map twice without being the headline: a disclosed 9.3% beneficial stake in $NBIS, and the $AMD–Anthropic deal ($5B investment, 2GW of chips) that openly copies NVDA's own playbook.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Unchanged: NVDA is the demand hub whose architecture choices (CPO, NVLink, memory specs) decide which suppliers win — the corpus's value is mapping those choices, not trading the hub. The week reinforced the frame twice over: the narrative war (delay rumors) happened at NVDA while the P&L damage and recovery happened in the supply chain.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Not the desk's trade. The reasons to own NVDA are whole-portfolio reasons; this corpus adds nothing to them beyond confirmation that its supply chain, not its narrative, is where the analyst's edge lives.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: For the map rather than the stock: rumor cycles that move supplier prices faster than facts, and the growing pattern of technical nuances being amplified into delay claims — which he flags as a structural information hazard for the whole complex.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch — hold as a core-portfolio decision outside this workflow, express the conviction through the suppliers. Re-rate only if he starts publishing NVDA-specific supply or pricing work.

memos.title: The crash gave the thesis its arithmetic
memos.dek: Through a 50% drawdown and a 31% snap-back day, the analyst published a checkable capacity model — and AMD's event this week could name the second customer chain.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: The most violent week in the corpus: the whole AI complex crashed on deleveraging (his own portfolio -49.4% on leverage, 320,000+ Korean margin accounts force-liquidated), then staged a historic single-day recovery with $SIVE up 30.9%. Through it, he published the most falsifiable Sivers work yet — a capacity-ramp model instead of a narrative.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: The model: assume Sivers gets just 10% of Win Semi's wafer capacity at 65% yield and a $50–75 ASP — that supports $341–512M of annual array revenue and, at management's 50–60%+ gross-margin target, roughly $205–307M of annual gross profit, against what he cites as a ~$1.1B market cap. That's 3.6–5.4x market-cap-to-gross-profit if the 2028 scenario lands; at a 15% allocation it drops to 2.4–3.6x. Demand-side, the CW bottleneck now has two independent confirmations: $LITE is buying CW lasers off the open market per its own earnings transcript, and $AMD is signing LTAs to secure CW capacity per TrendForce. His companion frame: $LITE went from $3B to $60B+ in two years by owning the EML chokepoint — $SIVE is positioned for the CW chokepoint at the valuation Lumentum started from.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Unchanged structure, sharpened math: a real bottleneck owned by a small company, multiple qualification tracks ($GFS, $JBL, Ayar, $POET, O-NET), and the NASDAQ listing as a non-fundamental re-rate catalyst. New this week: any qualified CW capacity that comes online is likely absorbed on current constraints — the demand side no longer depends on his advocacy.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: Everything from prior memos stays live: going-concern language, the Ningi short report, dilution, the integrated-laser kill-shot, and maximal messenger risk — he is heavily long and posting daily through a crash. The model itself imports three stacked assumptions (allocation, yield, ASP) from management guidance and his own estimates; miss any one and the multiple math decays fast. The AMD event cuts both ways — a non-optical MI500 route would remove the second-vendor leg.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate on the staggered plan — crash-day tranches were the plan working, not a new signal. After the snap-back, the next add wants either the AMD event confirming an Ayar/GF SCALE optical route (which maps $SIVE upstream) or a fresh red day. Kill-switches: AMD bypassing the CW chain, Win Semi assumptions failing at the next update, insider selling, or the listing slipping.

memos.title: The selloff was the entry; AEHR adds a read
memos.dek: Memory crashed on structurally good news and snapped back — while Aehr's NAND benchmark points, in his reading, straight at SanDisk.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: The verdict asked for a starter tranche 'into the current memory selloff only' — and the crash delivered it, hard: memory sold off on a week of confirmed LTAs and 20%+ DRAM hikes, then $SNDK snapped back 12.8% in the historic recovery day. New information arrived from an angle nobody was watching: $AEHR completed a wafer-level burn-in benchmark with a 'global leader in NAND flash' now evaluating a development agreement for HBM/NAND — which he reads as SanDisk, tying back to last quarter's HBF discussions.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Unchanged: NAND is in a verified upcycle, the $META LTA anchors demand, and HBF is the free option. The AEHR read, if confirmed, would be the first hardware-qualification evidence that the HBF roadmap is real rather than conference-slide material. The Meritz fulfillment math (60% range in 2027) now frames the whole memory book's upside window.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Higher torque to the NAND cycle than the flagship names, an undisclosed-terms LTA book that could surprise in either direction, and the HBF optionality — now with a possible qualification datapoint attached.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: Post-run volatility is violent in both directions, as the month proved. LTA terms remain undisclosed and could cap price capture the way Micron's ceilings do. Samsung/SK Hynix emergency NAND capex converting into 2027 oversupply is the cycle-killer. The AEHR identification is his inference, not a disclosure.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate — the selloff tranche was the plan executing. No adding into the snap-back; the add triggers are LTA pricing shown to reset with spot, or the AEHR development agreement confirmed as SanDisk. Kill-switches unchanged.

memos.title: Five times the company's own guide
memos.dek: The $471m/month figure anchoring the bull case is roughly five times what management guides to. Off accumulate.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $AAOI is the high-beta datacom optics name in the book — the one whose valuation argument has always been a forward revenue rate rather than current earnings.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: The case is that 800G and 1.6T shipments ramp hard into AI data centre demand, that AAOI reaches a $471m monthly revenue rate from the second half of 2027, and that a roughly $6bn market cap against that rate is absurdly cheap.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The near-term ramp is real and company-confirmed: Q1 revenue was a record $151.1m, up 51%, with Q2 800G shipments guided at nearly four times Q1 levels. The volume inflection is not in dispute.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Management guides Q2 2026 to $180-198m and the full year to roughly $1.1bn. A $471m monthly rate is about five times that run-rate, and it is presented in the source material as the company's own estimate.

Q2 is guided to non-GAAP EPS between -$0.03 and +$0.03 on 29-30% gross margin. At record revenue the business is at breakeven, so a one-times-forward-revenue multiple is only cheap against a top line that currently earns nothing.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: The ramp is real, the 2027 number is not underwritten by anyone but the bulls. Hold what exists, stop scaling in, and reopen the case only when management guides toward the rate the thesis assumes.

memos.title: The CPO read-through has no AMD behind it
memos.dek: Enters Core on score. The desk's interest is co-packaged optics adoption, and that rests on channel checks, not disclosure.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $AMD enters Core coverage on mention volume, largely as the presumed first customer for co-packaged optics among the [[accelerators]].

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: If AMD commits to CPO for Helios scale-up networking, it converts the [[photonics]] laser suppliers from a thematic bet into a scheduled one, with [[aaoi]] and [[sive]] the named beneficiaries.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Independently of the optics narrative, the accelerator business is compounding: Q1 data centre revenue of $5.8bn was up 57%, with Q2 guided to roughly $11.2bn plus or minus $300m, about 46% growth at the midpoint.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The CPO adoption claim traces to channel checks and a Rosenblatt note, not to any AMD disclosure. Helios and MI450 ship in the second half of 2026 on pluggable optics, with co-packaged optics described as a future-generation option — which puts the read-through in 2027 at the earliest.

Q2 results land 4 August against a guide already embedding 46% growth, making the near term a binary on execution.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch. Do not take a position into the print, and do not own AMD as a proxy for the photonics thesis — if AMD is worth owning it is as an accelerator business on its own numbers.

memos.title: A real business waiting for its AI quarter
memos.dek: Record revenue, two anchor customers prepaying for capacity, and a de-rating that prices the gap between now and 2028.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $AMKR is the largest US-headquartered outsourced assembly and test provider, and it enters coverage at the operator's request rather than on score — three mentions, ranked well outside the [[photonics]] and [[memory]] names this desk normally covers. It sits in the book as the advanced packaging link: the step where multiple dies become one package.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
Advanced packaging is a binding constraint on accelerator supply, and two of the most important customers in the industry have committed to Amkor's US capacity — a **$1.5B** agreement with $NVDA and a ten-year packaging partnership with $TSM.

The analyst's framing is that the market punished a name whose AI ramp is a year or two out while rewarding companies delivering acceleration today. He names Amkor explicitly as that example, and describes it as "more of a 2028 name" with separate ramps in 2027.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
Unlike most of this book's higher-conviction positions, the numbers here are reported rather than modelled. Amkor posted record second-quarter net sales of **$1.90 billion**, up 26% year on year, with $0.70 of diluted earnings per share — a profitable, growing business before any AI packaging revenue arrives.

That matters because it changes what a drawdown means. In [[sive]] or [[aaoi]] a de-rating tests a forecast; here it tests patience against a business that already works. Being paid in advance by $NVDA to build capacity is also the strongest form of demand evidence available — customers who prepay are not hedging.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The record quarter was led by Computing and Automotive & Industrial, not by the AI packaging ramp. The thing being bought is not yet the thing producing the revenue, and by the analyst's own timeline it will not be until 2028.

The $NVDA money is a prepayment for capacity expansion, so it lands in cash flow well before it lands in earnings — the same structure that turned up in the [[axti]] substrate agreements, and the same trap of reading a headline dollar figure as income.

OSAT is also a cyclical, capital-hungry, thin-margin industry by nature. If Computing softens before the AI ramp replaces it, the position carries the cycle without the story.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate, slowly, as a multi-year holding. The structural case is sound and unusually well-evidenced for this book, but the clock is long and the de-rating is not obviously irrational — the market is pricing two years of waiting. Quarterly tranches, no adding on partnership headlines, and treat any further drawdown as expected rather than as new information.

memos.title: Off the roster, with the deposit read corrected
memos.dek: Drops out of Core on score at rank 25. The Lumentum deposits are customer prepayments offset against future invoices, not reservation income.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $AXTI leaves the verdict roster this week on score, ranking 25th. Its last recorded desk stance was watch and no position was ever suggested.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: AXT supplies the indium phosphide substrates that [[lite]] and [[cohr]] turn into lasers, which makes it the upstream chokepoint of the chokepoint — one link further up than the [[photonics]] names the desk owns.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The long-term supplier agreement with Lumentum reserves a minimum annual indium phosphide commitment through 31 December 2031 and supports additional capacity if required. Being paid in advance to reserve capacity is what a genuine bottleneck looks like.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The agreement is two deposits of $43.5m, $87m in total, with the second only in calendar 2028. Both operate as shipment credits offset against future invoices, not fees — the cash arrives years before the revenue does.

No wafer volumes, pricing or capacity figures are disclosed, so the scale of the reservation cannot be sized from the filing. Concentration also rises: the small group of laser makers reserving the capacity are the only buyers of the output.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Leaves coverage without a position ever having been taken, which is the right outcome for a name whose entire attraction was a cash line that turns out to be deferred revenue. The exposure is better held through [[lite]].

memos.title: The prime that only appears by association
memos.dek: Enters Core on mentions, but every one of them is someone else's thesis. No Coherent-specific numbers in this corpus.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $COHR enters Core coverage as one of the three photonics primes with CPO laser visibility, alongside [[lite]] and [[sive]].

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: The same InP shortage that constrains [[lite]] constrains Coherent, and Coherent has reserved substrate capacity from [[axti]] to secure supply. If lasers are the chokepoint, the primes capture the pricing.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Structural exposure to the InP shortage with an established datacom franchise, at a valuation that fell about a third in a month alongside the rest of [[photonics]].

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Every mention in this corpus is by association — the substrate agreement, the Morgan Stanley visibility trio, another company's shortage commentary. There is no dedicated thesis with Coherent's own numbers.

Datacom sits inside a much larger, slower industrial business, so the shortage's effect on group earnings is diluted in a way it is not at a pure-play.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch. [[lite]] carries the same exposure at higher purity and with the numbers disclosed. Coherent earns a position when its datacom segment maths is sized separately, not before.

memos.title: The payer whose spending is funded
memos.dek: Enters Core as the strongest of the four capex payers — but only about 40% of that capex reaches the names this desk owns.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $GOOGL enters Core coverage as the [[hyperscalers]] name with the clearest link between what it spends and what it earns.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Capex funded out of an accelerating cloud business is more durable than capex funded out of a mature one, which makes Alphabet the most reliable demand signal in the group for everything downstream.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Q2 revenue of $119.8bn was up 24%, Google Cloud reached $24.8bn up 82%, quarterly capex hit a record $44.9bn, and the full-year guide rose to $195-205bn. The spend and the business behind it are moving together.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Roughly 60% of the capex goes to servers and 40% to data centres and networking equipment. Only that second slice reads through to optics and interconnect, so headline capex materially overstates the addressable pull for this book.

The stock fell about 5% on the capex raise despite a revenue beat, and has since rallied 12% in a week — the entry is not here.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: The accumulate case is sound and the timing is not. Wait for the next capex-driven derating rather than buying the rebound.

memos.title: Better customers, same funding question
memos.dek: Enters Core on an ARR revision to $4bn-plus with real counterparties — and the same capacity-funding gap as every neocloud.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $IREN enters Core coverage as the second [[neoclouds]] name in the book, a converted bitcoin miner rebuilding as an AI cloud.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Existing power and data centre shells convert to AI compute faster and cheaper than greenfield capacity, letting a miner reprice its asset base against AI demand.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The ARR target was revised to $4bn-plus on new AI cloud contracts, with Microsoft, Nvidia, Perplexity and Figure named as customers. That is a genuine step up in counterparty quality and the single substantive datapoint behind the tier promotion.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Most of the remaining mentions are drawdown-and-snapback breadth lists, which inflate the mention count without adding evidence.

Contracted ARR is not funded capacity — the same gap that moved [[nbis]] off accumulate applies here, with less disclosure behind it.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch. [[nbis]] already carries the neocloud exposure with more visibility. Doubling the leg is a sizing decision, not a reason to add a correlated second name.

memos.title: The capex was in the recap, the miss was not
memos.dek: Q2 EPS missed badly funding the same capex the desk reads as a demand signal. Supplier read-through intact, equity off accumulate.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $META sits in this book as the payer — held to validate that the capex funding the [[photonics]] and [[memory]] supply chain is actually being spent.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Hyperscaler capex is the demand signal for everything downstream, and Meta's 2026 guidance of $130-145bn is among the largest single commitments in the group. Owning the payer alongside the suppliers was the way to hold both ends of the same trade.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The capex commitment held and the low end of the range rose $10bn in a single quarter. As a demand signal for [[hyperscalers]] spend, nothing deteriorated.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Q2 EPS was $6.18 against roughly $7.14 expected, on $60.8bn of revenue and $31.1bn of quarterly capital expenditure, and the shares fell about 8%. Free cash flow is compressing under the buildout.

Part of the capex increase is memory cost inflation rather than incremental compute units, so the headline dollars overstate the unit demand reaching suppliers.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: The supplier read-through survives; the equity does not deserve accumulate while the market is derating it for the spending that creates that read-through. Holding Meta and holding Meta's suppliers have become opposite expressions of one view, and this desk already owns the supply side.

memos.title: Leaving at the margin peak
memos.dek: Drops out of Core on score at rank 21. Record DRAM revenue at 84.9% gross margin is a cycle peak, and only a fifth of volume is contracted.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $MU leaves the verdict roster this week on score, ranking 21st. Its last recorded desk stance was watch; [[sndk]] carried the [[memory]] exposure throughout.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: AI demand structurally repriced memory, and long-term supply agreements convert a notoriously cyclical business into something closer to a contracted one.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Fiscal Q3 DRAM revenue was a record $31.3bn, up 343% year on year at 84.9% consolidated gross margin, with 16 strategic customer agreements and remaining performance obligations above $5bn. The demand lock is contractual rather than anecdotal.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Only about 20% of DRAM and 30% of NAND volume is covered by those agreements, so roughly four fifths of DRAM volume remains exposed to spot pricing. The contracts smooth the cycle rather than remove it.

An 84.9% gross margin is a cycle peak, not a run-rate, and the agreements defend floor prices and volume rather than the pricing above the floor — which is the part currently carrying the earnings.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Exits coverage on rank, and the timing is not unwelcome. The structural memory case is intact; the entry point at peak margin was not, and [[sndk]] already expresses the upcycle with more torque.

memos.title: A financing story wearing a compute story's clothes
memos.dek: Power and contracts are landing; the funding gap between $399m of quarterly revenue and the capex plan is the actual risk. Off accumulate into the 12 August print.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $NBIS is the desk's [[neoclouds]] position — the way to own AI compute demand without owning a hyperscaler or a chip designer.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Nebius contracts power and capacity ahead of demand, converts it into annualised run-rate, and grows into a market where compute is scarce. Capacity secured today is revenue two to four quarters out.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The operating execution is visible: up to 1.2GW of power and land secured for an owned site in Pennsylvania, and more than 3GW expected under contract by year-end. For a neocloud the binding constraint is energised capacity, and that constraint is being cleared ahead of the revenue.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Q1 revenue was $399.0m, which annualises near $1.6bn against a full-year target of $3-3.4bn. Almost the entire guide sits in the second half and depends on capacity landing on schedule.

Capex plans run an order of magnitude above revenue, which makes the terms of the next capital raise a larger determinant of the equity return than GPU demand is.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Nothing is broken — but accumulate implies the risk being underwritten is demand, and it is not, it is financing. Hold into the 12 August print and let the H2 step-up show up before adding.

memos.title: The pipeline is not the revenue
memos.dek: Outside research put numbers against the Sivers story for the first time, and they point the other way. Stepping off accumulate until the 27 August interim.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $SIVE is the laser supplier at the centre of this desk's photonics book — the name most cited, most conviction-tagged, and now the one where the analyst's evidence and the company's filings disagree most sharply.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: The bull case is that Sivers supplies the InP lasers for co-packaged optics as [[photonics]] moves from pluggable modules to CPO, with [[poet]] as the interposer partner and a fab-light capacity model behind it. The forward maths circulating this week — 10% of a partner's wafer capacity supporting $341-512m of annual array revenue — is a modelled upper bound, not an order book.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The structural argument is unchanged and still good. Sivers and [[lite]] were the only two public laser suppliers named in the CPO programme that just drew a $300m US award to [[gfs]], which is real third-party validation of where the technology is going. If CPO happens on the timeline the industry is signalling, the laser supply is the chokepoint and there are very few suppliers.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Q1 net sales were SEK 61.9m, down 22% year on year. The $799m figure quoted as evidence is an opportunity pipeline, not backlog or revenue.

The [[poet]] wording upgrade read as a material timeline change resolves, in the only citable partnership language, to production readiness by end of 2026 with prototypes in the first half — a milestone, not an order. No volume, customer or ASP has been disclosed by either company.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Nothing here says the thesis is wrong; it says the thesis is still entirely forward-looking while the reported revenue is shrinking and the stock has halved in a month. Existing tranches stand, new size waits. The 27 August interim is the first thing that can settle it.

memos.title: Everything is built here, which is the problem
memos.dek: Enters Core on structural mentions. The least differentiated way to own a thesis whose entire edge is upstream.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $TSM enters Core coverage on mention volume generated by other companies' announcements rather than by any thesis about TSMC itself.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: TSMC manufactures the substrate on which this whole map is built, so exposure to AI compute is exposure to TSMC by definition.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The structural position is unassailable and the mentions reflect it — a ten-year advanced packaging partnership with [[amkr]], silicon-photonics volume revisions driving analyst estimates across the chain, CPO revenue showing up at test and metrology suppliers.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Being the common denominator is exactly what removes the edge. Every asymmetry this desk has found sits in small suppliers upstream, and TSMC's scale dilutes each of them to a rounding error.

None of the week's mentions constitute a TSMC-specific claim that could be right or wrong.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Watch. Own it as a core-portfolio decision if you want broad exposure, but this research produces no edge on it.

memos.title: The margin line and the 2028 line disagree
memos.dek: Record revenue and a return to profit, but the guided gross margin is flat — while the story being told is about 2028 capacity.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body:
$AAOI reported record Q2 revenue of $191.9M, up 86% year over year and 27% sequentially, with non-GAAP gross margin of 29.8% and a return to non-GAAP profitability at $0.06 per share. Fifth consecutive record quarter. The 800G product more than doubled sequentially.

The analyst's follow-up focused elsewhere: an ELSFP capacity plan of roughly 400,000 units a month in 2028, multiplied by an assumed price, producing close to $1.9B of new annualised revenue capacity.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The desk stays at wait, and the reason is the gap between those two paragraphs.

Q3 is guided to revenue of $255-290M with **non-GAAP gross margin of 29-30.5%** — flat at the midpoint against the 29.8% just delivered. Management separately describes 32-33% as the near-term margin. Guidance does not contain that expansion. On a ramp this steep, flat margin means the volume is being bought with mix and cost, which is what $0.06 of non-GAAP EPS on record revenue is telling you.

The 2028 arithmetic is a capacity plan multiplied by an assumed selling price, with no disclosed customer commitment attached. It may well happen. It is not evidence in the way a signed agreement is — compare the substrate LTAs at [[axti]], where the customer paid a deposit.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
The demand is real and the company is the volume incumbent in transceivers, with a genuine 1.6T ramp and a stated path into external light sources for co-packaged optics. If the mix shift lands, the margin structure improves mechanically rather than through cost discipline, and the operating leverage in this model is large.

There is also a policy option attached: a proposed United States restriction on new Chinese optical transceivers would hand share to a domestic manufacturer. It is a draft rule, not a published one — worth something, but not yet a catalyst.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The full-year figure near $1.1B implies a fourth quarter around $500M against a Q3 midpoint near $272M. That is close to a doubling in one quarter, on capacity the company itself describes as constrained. The $500M number is a residual of the annual guide, not a guided figure, and it is being quoted as though it were the latter.

Margins are the live risk: they went sideways this quarter and are guided sideways next quarter, while the equity has re-rated on a 2028 story. If Q3 gross margin fails to clear 30%, the thesis loses its nearest testable support.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Wait, at this price. The company is executing on volume and has not yet executed on margin, and the market is currently paying for 2028. The desk has recorded a dated claim on this: Q3 non-GAAP gross margin lands inside the guided 29-30.5% band rather than reaching 32-33%. That is checkable in December, and it is the number that decides the call.

memos.title: The filing says MI350, not MI450
memos.dek: AMD's own 10-Q attributes the 107% data-centre growth to EPYC and MI350. The CPO read-through stays a 2027 story.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $AMD sits in this book as a demand node — the desk's interest is whether its rack-scale systems adopt co-packaged optics, which would pull [[photonics]] volume forward.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: AMD is taking accelerator share with the Instinct line and moving to rack-scale with Helios. If those racks adopt co-packaged optics rather than pluggable modules, it converts a laser thesis into a schedule.

sections.heading: Why own it
