sections.body: The accelerator business is compounding on its own terms and does not need the optics story: data-centre revenue of $6.7bn in the quarter, up 107% year on year, with a stated expectation that the segment more than doubles again in 2027 and named commitments including a two-gigawatt Anthropic deployment.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The dates are the problem for this desk's purposes. The 10-Q attributes the quarter's growth to EPYC and MI350-series parts; Helios entered production with shipments starting only at the end of the third quarter, and the first gigawatt of the Anthropic deployment begins in the first half of 2027.

So the read-through to [[sive]] and [[aaoi]] is 2027 at the earliest, and the 2027 doubling is already the consensus case at this price — three quarters of carry with no proof in between.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: No desk action. If AMD is owned it is a whole-company accelerator call, not a photonics derivative. The trigger worth watching is a product disclosure naming co-packaged optics with a generation and a date.

memos.title: Up 71% on a rule that has not been written
memos.dek: Coherent still has no dedicated thesis in this corpus, and a large part of the move discounts a draft import ban with no published text.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $COHR is the other photonics prime alongside [[lite]], and the one whose datacenter exposure sits inside a much larger industrial business.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: The same indium phosphide shortage that drives [[lite]] drives Coherent, with the added kicker of a proposed US restriction on new Chinese optical transceivers that would hand share to Western suppliers.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The datacenter ramp is disclosed rather than inferred: third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $1.81bn, up 21% year on year, attributed to the datacenter business and higher communications demand, with fiscal Q4 guided to $1.91-2.05bn. That is a real, reported acceleration.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The margin structure is not a pure-play's. Non-GAAP gross margin was 39.6%, well below component peers, because industrial, telecom and materials dilute the datacenter mix — so a re-rating toward pure-play multiples assumes economics the reported segments do not yet produce.

The larger risk is what the move is discounting. The proposed ban on new Chinese optical transceivers exists as a draft rule with nothing published in the Federal Register, so scope, timing and exemptions cannot be verified. It is an option, not a catalyst, and it is being paid for as though it were the latter.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: No dedicated action, and specifically do not buy the ban. [[lite]] carries the same shortage at higher purity. Coherent earns a position on its own datacenter segment maths in the 12 August print, not on the sector's tape.

memos.title: The downgrade lasted one day
memos.dek: The desk cut $LITE to wait on 10 August on a stated condition. The 11 August print was the opposite of that condition, so the call goes back.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body:
$LITE was moved from accumulate to wait on 10 August, one day before fiscal Q4 results. The reasoning was explicit and narrow: the stock had run hard into a known event, and the exit trigger named was **an in-line print with unchanged capacity commentary**.

That is not what arrived. Revenue was $1.01B, up 109% year over year, with non-GAAP gross margin of 50.4% and non-GAAP operating margin of 36.6%. Guidance for the following quarter was raised to $1.225-1.275B with operating margin of 39.5-40.5% and EPS of $4.05-4.35 — the company's target operating model, reached more than a quarter early.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The named falsifier fired against the downgrade, so the downgrade is withdrawn. This memo records that as a desk error rather than a change in the world: the information that reversed the call was always going to arrive within twenty-four hours, and the trim bought nothing.

One correction to the analyst's read, which is running ahead of the filing. He frames the print as CPO validation. Management's own words place the ultra-high-power laser ramp in **the second half of calendar 2027** — Lumentum's fiscal 2028. What beat, and what is guided, is current datacom optics. The CPO leg is confirmed on timing, not yet on revenue, and nothing in these numbers or the guided quarter contains it.

The corroborating evidence sits one floor down: $AXTI has a signed long-term agreement with Lumentum backed by a $43.5M capacity reservation deposit. A customer prepaying a supplier for substrate capacity is a harder demand signal than the transcript language — see [[axti]] and [[photonics]].

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
Two engines with different clocks. The datacom optics business is delivering now, at a margin structure management said would take longer to reach. The CPO and external-light-source business is dated, sourced to the company, and starts in second-half calendar 2027 — so the position does not require the second engine to work in order to be underwritten on the first.

It is also the liquid, disclosed way to own the laser bottleneck. Where [[sive]] rests on a modelled capacity figure and $AAOI on a 2028 unit plan, Lumentum's version of the same thesis is reported quarterly with guidance attached.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The multiple is the risk, not the business. Annualising the guided EPS midpoint still leaves the shares near fifty times earnings, which prices continued execution rather than offering a discount to it.

The CPO timing is a company statement about a period more than a year away, and the same transcript that sharpened it could unsharpen it. The Greensboro indium phosphide capacity is a **conversion** of an existing gallium arsenide fab, which requires process transfer and customer requalification measured in quarters — so the supply gap management describes does not close on that asset inside fiscal 2027.

And the desk's own record here is now a data point: this name has been moved twice in a month, once wrongly.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Back to accumulate, as a correction rather than a fresh signal. Own it for the datacom optics that are already printing; treat the second-half-2027 laser ramp as unpaid-for optionality. What would change it: operating margin guided below 39.5% in any quarter before the ramp, or the 2027 timing slipping in a later call.

memos.title: The payer leaves the roster
memos.dek: Meta drops off the verdict roster on score. The supplier read-through is intact; the equity is still being derated for the spending that creates it.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $META is a demand node in this map — one of the four capex payers whose spending funds the [[hyperscalers]] leg of the supply chain.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Meta's capital spending is a leading indicator for accelerator, memory and optics demand. Owning the suppliers and owning the payer are, at this point, opposite expressions of the same view.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The spend is committed and large: $31.1bn of capital expenditure in the quarter and full-year guidance narrowed upward to $130-145bn. As a demand signal for this book it is unambiguous.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Free cash flow was $784m in the quarter. The buildout is consuming the cash generation that made Meta a self-funding compounder, and the shares are down roughly a quarter over the past year while the suppliers they fund have multiplied.

The disclosure also gives capex dollars and nothing else — no accelerator mix, no useful-life assumption — so the figure cannot be converted into unit demand for any specific supplier.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: No position. The desk already owns the supply side, which is the same view expressed where the cash is arriving rather than leaving.

memos.title: Off the roster two days before the print
memos.dek: Nebius drops out of the verdict roster on score as the analyst's own coverage turns bearish. The Q2 report on 12 August is the test.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $NBIS leaves the verdict roster on priority score, not on a stance change — it is still Core tier, and the desk still has no neocloud position.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: Nebius rents AI compute at scale, with energised capacity as the binding constraint and contracted demand well ahead of delivery. The bear case, which the analyst himself has now started writing, is that this is a financing story before it is a compute story.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Nothing in the operating story has broken. Capacity is described as fully contracted, capex has been guided up to $20-25bn, and the customer roster and NVIDIA's equity stake are real third-party validation.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The disclosure is thin where it matters. The filings give no contracted megawatts, no delivery schedule and no customer names, so the sold-out claim cannot be independently sized in either direction.

And the balance sheet carries the risk: first-quarter revenue of $399m against capex guided to $20-25bn, funded by $4.3bn of convertibles and secured debt at SOFR plus 250 basis points. Any slip in customer ramp lands on financing terms, not on cash.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: No position, and no verdict coverage until the score recovers. The 12 August print is the thing to read — specifically whether prepayments are being presented as demand.

memos.title: Still a wording change, not an order
memos.dek: POET leaves the verdict roster on score. The interposer story is unchanged and still carries no revenue.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $POET is the optical interposer partner in the [[sive]] story — the piece that would put Sivers lasers into a packaged product.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: If co-packaged optics scales, the interposer is a real position in the stack and POET is one of very few public ways to own it. The bull case turns on the production timeline with Sivers lasers by the end of 2026.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: The balance sheet removes the usual small-cap risk: working capital of roughly $419m against about $8.8m of quarterly operating cash burn funds years of runway without a forced raise.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
There is no product revenue. First-quarter revenue of $503,389 was non-recurring engineering, and the upgrade in language from production-readiness to production is a company statement with no shipped volume behind it.

Existing holders paid for the runway: shares outstanding rose about 74% over the year, including a 20.7m-share placement in January.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: No position, and if it is ever taken it is option-sized. The trigger remains a purchase order or a revenue-recognising shipment, not a press-release verb.

memos.title: The insider buying was real. So was the selling.
memos.dek: The feed reported the chief executive's purchase and omitted roughly 1.2 million shares sold by two board members after the lock-up expired.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body:
$SIVE remains the analyst's highest-conviction name and his largest position. The desk has held it at wait since 3 August, on the grounds that every number in the thesis is modelled rather than reported.

This week the desk checked the insider-transaction disclosure that the feed cited, and found it materially incomplete.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The reported story was insider buying into weakness — the chief executive purchasing 70,000 shares. That is accurate and it happened.

What was not reported: after the lock-up from the April directed share issue expired on 16 July, the **chairman sold 275,000 shares**, and a **board member sold 950,000 shares** through his own vehicle, with a venture holder liquidating alongside. Net insider flow is roughly 1.2 million shares out against 70,000 in.

This is the second time the desk has found the feed reporting one side of a disclosure on this name, and it matters more here than elsewhere because the position is the analyst's largest — every reiteration is also an advertisement. The supply-chain logic remains strong; the reporting around it is not neutral.

The underlying numbers have not moved. Last reported quarter net sales were SEK 61.9M, down 22% year over year. The $799M figure repeated in the feed is an **opportunity pipeline**, not an order book, and no shipped indium phosphide laser volume has ever been disclosed.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
The chokepoint argument survives all of the above. Continuous-wave indium phosphide lasers are a genuine bottleneck, few suppliers exist, and Sivers sits on qualification tracks at several customers at once — a structure of partially independent shots rather than one design win. The ecosystem evidence keeps improving around it: $LITE and $COHR both prepaid for substrate capacity at [[axti]], and $AAOI cited a demand imbalance with lasers named as the constraint.

That is real corroboration for the theme. It is not yet corroboration for this company's revenue.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The whole thesis converts or fails to convert on **27 August**, when the Q2 interim report lands. It is the first hard datapoint in the entire story, and the shares have re-rated hard going into it.

Governance is now a live item rather than a footnote, given the direction of insider flow after a lock-up expiry. And the modelled revenue figure circulating in the feed rests on wafer-allocation maths that cannot be checked against anything the company has reported.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Hold, add nothing before 27 August. Paying a re-rated price for information that arrives in fifteen days is the specific mistake this desk made on [[lite]] last week in the opposite direction. The desk has recorded two dated claims here, both judgeable in early September: that the interim report will not disclose InP product revenue as a distinct figure, and that net sales come in below SEK 100M.

memos.title: Buying the boring leg while the exciting ones re-rate
memos.dek: Everything on this map is built at TSMC. After a week in which the suppliers rose 48-77%, that stops being a reason to ignore it.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: $TSM is the foundry every name in this book depends on, which is exactly why the desk has treated it as scenery until now.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body: The analyst's objection — that TSMC is the least differentiated way to own the AI buildout — was correct while the small suppliers were cheap. It stops being correct when they are not. First-half revenue was up 35.6% year on year with June alone up 67.9%, and the shares are down about 7% on the month while the [[photonics]] complex ran hard.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
Three things no other name here offers. Monthly revenue disclosure, so the demand curve can be checked every thirty days instead of every quarter. No qualification risk, no dilution risk, no single-customer risk. And a valuation that is a fraction of what the suppliers now carry per unit of revenue.

It does the same job in the book that [[jbl]] does: ballast bought deliberately when the high-variance legs are expensive.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Advanced packaging is easing rather than tightening. Industry reporting has the CoWoS supply-demand gap narrowing from roughly 20% to 10% by the end of 2026 as capacity expands toward about 200,000 wafers a month by end-2027. A bottleneck that resolves is a bottleneck that stops paying, and TSMC's pricing power on packaging goes with it.

The second risk is that this is a large-cap and behaves like one — it will not produce the returns the small suppliers can.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Starter position, quarterly tranches, sized as ballast. Use the monthly revenue release as the running check rather than waiting on quarters.

memos.title: The floor under the laser trade
memos.dek: Two laser makers have now prepaid $AXTI for indium phosphide substrate capacity. That is harder evidence than anything else in the photonics stack.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body:
$AXTI makes the compound semiconductor substrates — indium phosphide and gallium arsenide wafers — that the lasers in this book are grown on. It sits one layer below $SIVE, $LITE and $COHR in [[photonics]], and the desk dropped coverage of it earlier this month. That was wrong, and this memo restores it.

The reason is two signed long-term agreements. Lumentum agreed to pay a **$43.5M deposit** as a capacity reservation. Coherent signed earlier with a **$22.3M reservation payment**.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
Almost every number carrying this sector is modelled. Sivers' capacity revenue figure is a projection. AOI's 2028 external-light-source revenue is a unit plan times an assumed price. Lumentum's CPO ramp is a dated statement about the second half of calendar 2027.

The AXT agreements are a different class of evidence: a customer moving cash to a supplier, in advance, to secure supply it expects to need. Companies do not prepay for capacity they are unsure about. That makes the substrate layer the most concretely evidenced position in the entire photonics stack — and it is evidence about the whole theme, not just this company, because it tells you what the laser makers themselves believe about their own volumes.

It is also the classic supply-chain shape: when the bottleneck is lasers, the bottleneck under the bottleneck is the wafer they are grown on, and there are very few qualified sources.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
Multi-customer by construction. AXT does not need any single laser maker's design win to convert — it needs the category to ship, and it now has two of the largest names contracted with cash down. That is a materially better risk shape than a single-qualification bet.

The evidence also compounds in public: each additional LTA is a disclosed event, so the thesis updates on facts rather than on commentary.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The tape is the risk. This name has moved an extraordinary distance over the past year, so the market is not handing anyone this idea — the position must be sized as if a good business can still be a poor entry.

Substrate is a capital-intensive, historically cyclical business with real competition, including Chinese suppliers moving up the stack. A reservation deposit secures capacity but does not guarantee the customer draws against it. And the desk should note its own categorisation error here: this company is filed under memory in the store, when what it actually sells is compound substrate material.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate, scaling in on weakness rather than chasing strength. Own the layer beneath the laser trade, where the demand is contracted in cash rather than modelled in a spreadsheet. What would change it: a customer failing to draw against a reservation, or a competing substrate supplier qualifying at Lumentum or Coherent.

memos.title: Someone else's earnings are not your datapoint
memos.dek: CoreWeave and Supermicro printed enormous numbers. $IREN has published nothing since March and does not report until 16 September.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: A very loud week for the neocloud theme and a silent one for $IREN itself. CoreWeave disclosed a backlog above $100B, Supermicro guided FY27 revenue far above consensus, and $RIOT announced a large multi-year contract with Anthropic. The analyst read all three through to IREN and the other colocation names.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The desk stays at wait, on a narrow point: none of those numbers are IREN's.

The last IREN disclosure covered the March quarter, when revenue was $144.8M — **Bitcoin mining $111.2M, AI Cloud Services $33.6M** — with a net loss of $247.8M. The AI business is real and growing quickly, and it is still under a quarter of the revenue line. The contracted run-rate ambition the company has described requires roughly a thirtyfold scaling of that smaller segment.

The contracts behind it are genuine and large: a five-year agreement with NVIDIA and a further multi-billion GPU services agreement with Microsoft. What is not disclosed is contracted megawatts by customer or a delivery schedule, so the pace of conversion cannot be checked from outside — which is exactly what a read-through from someone else's backlog is being used to guess at.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
The demand evidence around the theme keeps getting stronger and it is not coming from promotional sources — it is coming from other companies' filed results. IREN owns powered land and has signed counterparties most of the colocation cohort cannot reach.

If the AI Cloud segment converts on anything like the stated pace, the current revenue mix becomes irrelevant quickly, and the mining base funds the transition in the meantime.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The financing shape is the risk. This is a capital-intensive buildout carrying a large quarterly loss, where any slip in customer ramp lands on a financed balance sheet rather than on cash. Revenue recognition timing on prepayments is worth watching — the operative question is whether prepaid capacity is being read as delivered demand.

And the theme is now crowded on read-through rather than disclosure, which is how a sector gets priced ahead of its own numbers.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Wait until 16 September. The read-through has already been paid for in the names that actually reported. The desk has recorded two dated claims judgeable at the end of September: that AI Cloud Services is still under half of total revenue in the Q4 print, and that per-customer contracted megawatts remain undisclosed.

memos.title: Owning the wrong half of memory
memos.dek: The desk held NAND through $SNDK and stayed off DRAM on multiple discipline. The tight market was DRAM the whole time.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: The desk has carried memory exposure through $SNDK since 16 July and has passed on $MU twice on the same reasoning: a cycle where the seller sets the price is the wrong moment to underwrite a multiple. This memo reverses that.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
Two facts make the earlier call wrong rather than merely early.

The first is scale. Micron's last reported quarter put revenue at **$41.46B**, against $23.86B the quarter before and $9.30B a year earlier, with data centre alone above **$25B** — an annualised run-rate over $100B — and the following quarter guided near $50B. That is not a company whose multiple needs defending; it is the most profitable link in the chain this book maps.

The second is which market is actually tight. $SNDK expresses NAND. The structural shortage is in DRAM and HBM, where server contract prices are set to rise **13-18% quarter on quarter in 3Q26** with long-term agreements capping the increase, and HBM contract prices are expected multiples higher in 2027 against RDIMM bit supply growing only 15-20%. Supply sets that price, not demand — which is precisely the condition the desk said it was waiting for.

The analyst has been right on memory for months and consistently under-argues it, posting the bottleneck as unchanged background rather than as the earnings event it has become.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
The pricing mechanism is contractual and dated, not sentiment. Long-term agreements cap the upside quarter to quarter, which also means they carry it forward: the 2027 reset is a scheduled event rather than a forecast.

It is also the cleanest expression on this map of the constraint everything else in the book is derivative of. [[memory]] sits under every accelerator in [[accelerators]], and unlike the photonics names the demand is already in the reported numbers rather than in a pipeline.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
This is the most cyclical position in the book and it is being added late, after the earnings inflection is visible to everyone. A memory cycle turns on supply response, and every producer is now incentivised to add capacity.

The second risk is doubling up by accident. $SNDK and $MU are not the same trade — NAND and DRAM tighten for different reasons — but they will correlate hard in a drawdown, and the combined memory weight is the thing to size against, not either position alone.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate, in quarterly tranches, as the DRAM and HBM leg alongside the existing NAND leg rather than instead of it. The exit signal is not a demand miss — it is the first quarter long-term agreement pricing stops rising.

memos.title: Right thesis, wrong week
memos.dek: $MTSI holds at accumulate one week after initiation and immediately underwater. The sector de-rated; the numbers did not.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: MACOM entered Core coverage last week on the strongest operating numbers on the roster and the thinnest analyst file. It is now well below the initiation level. Nothing company-specific caused that, and the stance is unchanged — but the drawdown deserves to be recorded rather than smoothed over.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The case is still the margin line, and it is filed rather than argued.

Fiscal Q3 revenue was **$342.2M, up 35.8%** year on year, with fiscal Q4 guided to **$415-425M** — another 21-24% sequential step — on a record **1.6 book-to-bill**. Adjusted gross margin is guided to **60-61%**, roughly double $AAOI's and ten to thirty points above everyone else in the layer, because MACOM sells content into the module rather than assembling it.

He argued it directly this week as part of the broader shortage, alongside $LITE and $AAOI, citing an optical supply chain where "the entire supply chain is out of stock" across laser chip, PCB, carrier board and packaging.

What happened to the price was a whole-sector event. The optical complex de-rated together this week while [[memory]] names ran — a rotation, not a revision.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
It is the component layer of [[photonics]] rather than the assembly layer, so it participates in the 800G and 1.6T ramp without carrying module price competition.

A record book-to-bill is hard to dress up: orders are running well ahead of shipments across all three end markets, not only datacenter.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The pm seat's advice to size this as an initiation rather than a conviction was correct, and is the only reason this drawdown is uncomfortable rather than damaging. That is the argument for position sizing generally.

The thin analyst file still cuts both ways: there is no bear case in this corpus to push against, so the desk is underwriting on company disclosure alone.

And a record book-to-bill is a peak indicator as often as a leading one. If the datacenter step-up was pull-forward, it shows up as book-to-bill falling back through 1.0 before it shows up in revenue.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate, unchanged, but no second tranche yet. The desk is already expressing this week's optical de-rating through $COHR, and buying two optical names on one idea in one week is concentration wearing conviction's clothes.

memos.title: The tooling is ready. The customers are not.
memos.dek: $LPK.DE enters Core the same week its customers pushed glass substrate start-up out to 2028.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: LPKF sells LIDE laser systems that structure glass — the tooling step a glass-substrate maker buys before it can produce anything. It enters Core coverage this week and is re-categorised from materials into [[glass]], where it joins $GLW as only the second name in the layer.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The timing is the story, and it is unhelpful.

The most recent thesis in the file is bearish: Samsung Electro-Mechanics has delayed its semiconductor glass substrate investment on a bottleneck in customer reliability evaluations of prototypes, revising the start of operations to **2028**, with SKC also pushing back. That is the analyst reporting a delay in his own theme.

For equipment this matters more than it does for a substrate supplier, not less. The tool order lands before the substrate line runs, so a customer moving its start date right moves LPKF's revenue event right with it — and there is no partial credit. The stock is down about 12% on the month, which is the market reading the same disclosure.

Sixteen accumulated mentions is what puts this name in Core. That is attention gathered over months, not conviction expressed this week, and the re-categorisation into a near-empty layer flatters its rank further.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
Glass substrates are a real layer of the 2028-2029 packaging roadmap and LPKF is the Western tooling name for it. A delay is not a cancellation: reliability evaluation bottlenecks are the normal shape of a qualification cycle, and the programmes were revised rather than shelved.

When it does turn, equipment turns first.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
A second delay pushes the revenue event beyond any reasonable holding period for a company this small, and the file contains no order to anchor against — only timeline commentary.

There is also a concentration problem the map hides: if glass substrate adoption is decided by two or three Korean customers, this is a two-or-three-customer stock wearing a supply-chain-layer badge.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Wait. This is a name to own on an order, not on a theme. The trigger is a disclosed LIDE system order from a named substrate customer with a delivery year attached.

memos.title: A trust is not a company
memos.dek: $CCXI is back in the top fifteen on humanoid enthusiasm and the desk still passes. The S-4 has not been filed publicly, and the price is a large premium to cash.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Churchill Capital Corp XI re-enters the Core top fifteen this week after the Unitree listing reset humanoid sentiment. The desk re-initiates coverage at pass. It has never carried a position and will not open one at this price against this structure.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The commercial argument for Agility is reasonable and got better this week.

Unitree listed publicly and closed far above its IPO valuation, giving the sector its first major public benchmark and suggesting appetite for pure-play humanoids well beyond what was assumed. The analyst bought between **0.25% and 0.75%** of the float and argues Agility is a relative laggard to that comparable. His operating point is also the right one: Digit targets commercial logistics inside $AMZN and $MELI warehouses rather than general-purpose capability, and warehouse automation does not require backflips. Deployments with Schaeffler, GXO, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada and Mercado Libre are real.

The instrument is the problem, not the company. $CCXI is a **pre-close special purpose acquisition company**. The Agility combination was announced **24 June 2026** at roughly **$2.5B**, with more than **$620M** of expected gross proceeds, and the Form S-4 was only **confidentially submitted**. Closing still requires public filing, SEC effectiveness, a shareholder vote, regulatory clearances and exchange listing before the ticker becomes **AGLT**.

Until the S-4 goes effective there are no audited Agility financials to read and no way to know redemption levels. Those two unknowns determine what a share actually represents.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
Agility is the most credible US pure-play humanoid asset available to a public investor, with named industrial customers running real deployments rather than demonstrations. If humanoids become a compute vertical, this is one of very few direct ways to hold it.

That case does not expire with this note. It resumes post-close, on disclosed unit economics.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The price is the risk. The shares trade at a substantial premium to a typical trust value, which means a buyer today pays well above cash for an option on a deal that has not publicly filed. If the deal breaks, the floor is redemption at trust — materially below the current price.

The deployments are disclosed as programmes rather than volumes, so the per-robot compute, memory and sensor content that would justify a read-through into this desk's map remains unquantified.

And there is a bias check worth stating plainly: the analyst holds a position sized in percent-of-float and is publicly arguing the comparable upward. That is not a reason to dismiss the idea, but it is a reason not to mistake enthusiasm for underwriting.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Pass. If the exposure is wanted, wait for the S-4 to go effective and buy AGLT once redemptions are known — accepting a worse headline price for a knowable balance sheet.

memos.title: Nothing to review for three weeks
memos.dek: $INTC leaves the verdict roster. The 14A schedule has not moved and neither has the analyst's attention.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Intel drops off the verdict roster on score. It carried a wait stance and no position, and there have been no new analyst theses on it since late July.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The reason for coverage was always the foundry option, and the disclosed schedule has not changed: 14A risk production in **2027**, high volume in **2028**. External foundry revenue is therefore not a 2026 or 2027 event, which puts it outside the horizon this map is built for.

Retiring the verdict is not a downgrade. It is an accurate statement that the desk has nothing new to say and that continuing to publish a weekly stance on an unchanged file would be manufacturing coverage.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
A Western leading-edge foundry alternative has strategic value that a quarterly file does not capture, and government and customer interest in one is real.

If 14A lands on schedule with a named external customer, the option reprices quickly.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: It remains a multi-year whole-company turnaround where the AI-supply-chain read-through is the smallest part of the story. Owning it for this map's reasons is owning the wrong 90% of the business.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Off the roster. It returns to coverage on a named external 14A customer with committed volume — not before.

memos.title: Still waiting on 16 September
memos.dek: $IREN leaves the roster with the same gap it had a week ago: no disclosure of its own.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: IREN drops off the verdict roster on score, carrying the same wait stance it has held throughout. No position was ever taken.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
Nothing has changed since the 12 August note, which is the point. The last IREN disclosure still covers the March quarter — revenue $144.8M, of which AI Cloud Services was $33.6M — and the company does not report again until **16 September**.

Everything that moved the name in the interim was someone else's filing. Retiring the verdict here avoids the specific failure mode this desk was built to resist: publishing a weekly stance that is really a summary of other companies' results.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
Powered land and grid interconnection are the genuinely scarce inputs in [[neoclouds]], and IREN holds both with counterparties most of the cohort cannot reach.

The AI Cloud segment is growing quickly off a small base, and the mining business funds the transition.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: Capital-intensive buildout carrying a large quarterly loss, with any customer ramp slip landing on a financed balance sheet. Contracted megawatts per customer are still undisclosed, so conversion pace cannot be checked from outside.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Off the roster until it publishes. Reconsider after 16 September, on AI Cloud Services as a share of total revenue and on disclosed contracted megawatts.

memos.title: Everything went right, which is the problem
memos.dek: $LITE goes to wait. Nothing broke — the business is compounding faster than plan, and that is now fully in the price.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Lumentum steps down from accumulate to wait after a year in which it did almost nothing wrong. This is a valuation call, not a business call, and it is worth being explicit about that distinction because the two get conflated constantly.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The operating record keeps improving.

Lumentum crossed **50% non-GAAP gross margin** a full quarter ahead of its own timeline, while shipping record 800G volume and starting 1.6T module production. Fiscal Q4 revenue was **$1.01B, up 109%** year on year, at a **36.6%** non-GAAP operating margin. Fiscal Q1 FY27 is guided to **$1.225-1.275B** with non-GAAP EPS of **$4.05-4.35**, against $3.23 just delivered.

That internal capacity scaling faster than planned is also the most useful datapoint in the whole [[photonics]] file, because it reframes the shortage. If the best operator in the layer is running ahead of schedule, the laser bottleneck is a merchant-supply problem, not an industry yield problem — which is bullish for anyone with in-house capacity and harsher on anyone buying on the open market.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
It remains the highest-quality operator in the optical layer, with the margin structure to prove it and demand visibility that now extends years rather than quarters.

Nothing in this note argues for selling. The desk's August entry is comfortably ahead of the benchmark and stays open.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The asymmetry is gone. At a guided $5B annualised run-rate and roughly 40% operating margin, Lumentum is priced as a finished AI winner rather than the turnaround the desk originally bought.

That changes the shape of the downside. It no longer requires the thesis to break — a single hyperscaler order-timing slip against a very high bar is enough. When a stock is priced for perfect execution, perfect execution stops being an edge and becomes the minimum entry requirement.

This downgrade is also deliberately made ahead of the $NVDA print, which is the sector-wide risk event sitting under every name in this book.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Wait. Hold what is held, stop adding. Accumulate comes back on a drawdown driven by sector multiple compression rather than by a Lumentum-specific order slip — or on a fiscal Q2 guide that shows the run-rate is still being underestimated.

memos.title: The one that owns the bottleneck
memos.dek: $COHR goes to accumulate. Every piece of news this week says indium phosphide is the constraint — and Coherent is the only name here that makes its own.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Coherent moves from wait to accumulate. This is the desk's own call rather than the analyst's: he referenced Coherent twice this week and both were back-references rather than arguments. That absence is the opportunity.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
Read this week's news as one story and the conclusion is hard to avoid.

$AXTI reported the largest indium phosphide price increase on record, the fourth consecutive quarterly hike, with suppliers saying money alone will not secure material. Elazr's general manager told an investor conference that "the entire supply chain is out of stock" and expects the shortage to run for years across laser chip, PCB, carrier board and packaging capacity. $AAOI says it is sold out well beyond next year. $LITE says the same.

The binding constraint in AI optics is InP and laser capacity. Coherent is the one company in this layer that owns that constraint instead of buying it: it **doubled six-inch indium phosphide capacity ahead of plan** and took datacenter and communications to **79% of Q4 revenue, up 59%** year on year. Keeping InP lasers in-house is an allocation decision, and it makes merchant supply scarcer for everyone else in [[photonics]].

The delivered numbers are not the problem either: record fiscal Q4 revenue of **$2.05B, up 34%**, FY26 revenue of **$7.12B, up 22.5%**, non-GAAP EPS up **59% to $5.61**, and fiscal Q1 FY27 guided to **$2.2-2.4B** with non-GAAP EPS of **$1.85-2.05**.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
Vertical integration is worth more in a shortage, not less, and the market is currently pricing it as worth less.

Coherent beat on every line and the shares fell — the same reaction Cisco and Applied Materials drew in the same week. The group is being repriced on gross margin rather than on growth, and Coherent guides **39.5-41.5%**, roughly ten points below $LITE. That gap is the entire bear case, and it is also the reason the vertically integrated name can be bought at a discount to the pure-play optics leader while holding the scarce asset.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The margin gap may be structural rather than temporary. If in-house InP is genuinely advantaged, it should show up as datacenter gross margin expanding; if it does not, the integration argument collapses into a lower-margin version of the peers and the discount is deserved.

This is also a contrarian entry into a sector de-rating that is still in progress. Buying a group the market is actively repricing means accepting that the timing will probably look wrong before it looks right.

And the whole optical complex now carries a single shared event risk in the $NVDA print.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate, half-size here. The second half goes below the current level or in the session after $NVDA reports. This is the desk rotating out of names that have already priced the shortage and into the one that has not.

memos.title: A very good model is not yet a very good quarter
memos.dek: $SNDK goes to wait after the investor day. The margin targets are real and verified; one load-bearing number in the bull summary is not.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Sandisk steps down from accumulate to wait. The business case got stronger this week. The price got stronger faster, and one figure being circulated does not appear in the company's own disclosure.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
What Sandisk actually guided at its 2026 investor day, verified against the release:

For **FY2028 through FY2030**, non-GAAP gross margins to sustain at **approximately 80%**, non-GAAP operating margins at **approximately 75%**, and adjusted free cash flow margin at **approximately 50%** after taxes, capex and working capital. Revenue to grow **mid-to-high teens**, consistent with bit growth. New Business Model agreements are signed with **eight customers**, covering **approximately 50% of bits in FY2027** and **approximately two-thirds in FY2028**, built on committed volumes, minimum financial guarantees and structured pricing.

That is a genuine attempt to engineer the cycle out of a cyclical business, and the independent corroboration is there: Phison's CEO expects 2027 capacity constraints more severe than 2026, on the logic that upstream suppliers need up to four years from plant construction to production.

One number does not check out. The claim that minimum contracted revenue reaches **$93B** appears in the bull summary but **not in Sandisk's investor day release**, which discloses no total committed-revenue figure at all. The desk could not source it and is not underwriting it. It may exist in the presentation materials; it is not company-confirmed in the announcement, and it is doing a lot of work in the valuation argument being built on top of it.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
The NBM structure is the most credible mechanism anyone in memory has put forward for making margins durable, and the demand side is corroborated independently of management.

Nothing here argues for exiting the core position. The [[memory]] shortage is real and multi-year.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
An approximately 80% sustained gross margin has no precedent in NAND's history. The contracts are a plausible mechanism for it, but they are a mechanism presented at an investor day, not a delivered result — and the market repriced roughly four years of that model in five sessions.

Accumulate means add. Adding after a move of that size means paying for flawless execution through fiscal 2030 up front, on a model whose most quotable supporting number the desk cannot source.

The honest test is contract renewal, not demand commentary. Committed volumes only protect margin if the committed price holds.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Wait. Take the August dip-buy tranche off into this strength and keep the core. New money returns when an NBM renewal is disclosed at pricing consistent with the model, or when the price gives back a meaningful part of this move.

memos.title: Twenty-nine bull arguments, no delivery
memos.dek: $XFAB is retired at pass. The CPO and 800V exposure is real; a year of design wins has not turned into revenue, and the desk carried it too long.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: X-FAB leaves coverage at pass. It never carried a dated desk entry, which is itself part of the lesson: it was held on the analyst's conviction rather than on the desk's own, and nothing in the calls ledger records it. Nothing is being stamped as an exit, because there was never an entry to close.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
The file is unusually one-sided. He has argued X-FAB **29 times and every single one is bull** — including a high-conviction add in early August after earnings that he said proved the bear posts wrong, confirming CPO and 800V exposure with design wins that should drive a rerating "once the ramp arrives".

The exposure is genuine. X-FAB is a real specialty foundry with real silicon carbide, gallium nitride and [[photonics]] positioning, and a sellside upgrade earlier in the summer cited strengthening lead-customer demand.

The delivery is the problem. Over the same twelve months in which $LITE, $AAOI and $AXTI all rose by multiples on the identical CPO and 800V thesis, X-FAB fell. A photonics-adjacent foundry that declines while the entire photonics complex re-rates is not a mispricing waiting to correct. It is the market telling you the design wins are not converting to revenue on any timeline an operator can actually hold.

He has not argued it once since the end of July. That silence is the same conclusion, reached quietly.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
If CPO volumes arrive at the specialty-foundry layer, X-FAB is positioned for them, and the underlying automotive and industrial base is not going away.

That case can be re-underwritten later. It just has to be re-underwritten from reported revenue rather than from design-win commentary.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The specific failure mode to record: "rerating once the ramp arrives" has been the argument for a year, and the ramp date has moved every time. A thesis whose payoff is always one catalyst away is not falsifiable, and an unfalsifiable thesis cannot be sized.

There is a scoring lesson too. Twenty-nine bull arguments push a name up the priority score regardless of whether any of them proved out, because the score measures the analyst's posting behaviour, not outcomes. This is the clearest case yet of that gap.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Pass, coverage closed. Re-underwrite only from a reported quarter with disclosed CPO or 800V revenue and a raised full-year guide — printed numbers, not design wins.

memos.title: "I can't see how anyone can be bearish"
memos.dek: $AAOI stays at wait. The demand is real and the analyst is at maximum conviction — while his own stated entry sits far below the current price.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Applied Optoelectronics drew nine new posts this week, the most of any name on the roster, and the most emphatic language of the year. The stance does not move. This is the week's sharpest disagreement between the analyst file and the desk.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
His Rosenblatt summit notes are the strongest version of the bull case, and they are worth taking seriously.

AOI expects to be paid premiums for US production of 800G and 1.6T, which lifts ASP and margin; it has several long-term agreements on the table but does not want capacity blocked by a single customer; it is sold out at least through the second half of next year; it already has 300-400mW lasers; and it expects margins above 40% once CPO arrives, which he reads as the trigger for a rerating. He also argues AOI could approach or pass $LITE on revenue in early 2028 if it executes its capacity plan, on a far smaller valuation.

The accounting has not caught up to the narrative. The reiterated roughly **$1.1B FY26** target requires Q4 revenue near **$485M** against a Q3 guide midpoint of **$272M** — a **78% sequential step in one quarter**, off $343M of first-half revenue. Q2 non-GAAP EPS was **$0.06** on $191.9M of revenue, so profitability is one cent thick, and Q3 gross margin is guided to **29-30.5%**, roughly twenty points below $LITE's. Management guided more than **$70M** of 1.6T revenue in Q4, which would be its first material 1.6T quarter — a ramp beginning, not a ramp proven.

A company whose entire year rests on one quarter nearly doubling, with no earnings cushion beneath it, is a company about which reasonable people can be bearish.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
The demand visibility is not in dispute. Being sold out into 2027 with US-production premiums available is a genuinely strong position, and if CPO lifts margins above 40% the rerating case is real.

There is also a tell worth using: the analyst says he is waiting for a much lower price to add. The most bullish voice in the file has a stated entry well below spot.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The margin structure is the risk, not the demand. At roughly 30% gross margin and one cent of quarterly EPS, a revenue miss has nothing underneath it — the same miss at $LITE or $MTSI is absorbed by margin that AOI does not have.

Qualification at 1.6T remains a quarterly event risk with a hyperscaler customer base, and the Q4 concentration makes a single slipped qualification a full-year miss.

Certainty language is itself a warning sign. "I can't see how anyone can be bearish" names no falsifier, and a thesis with no falsifier cannot be sized.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Wait. Use his number rather than his conviction: a limit meaningfully below spot, sized as a starter given the margin structure. If Q4 lands near $485M the entry is missed — accept that instead of paying up on faith.

memos.title: His favourite long, six days from a print
memos.dek: $SIVE stays at wait. The highest-conviction post of the week rests partly on two claims the primary record does not support.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Sivers drew the analyst's only high-conviction post of the week, calling it his favourite high-beta optical long. The stance does not move, and the reason is specific rather than general.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
His case has four supports. Two hold up well.

Sivers supplies lasers into $JBL pluggables, $POET and O-Net optical engines, Ayar optical I/O and $GFS photonic foundry work across NPO, pluggable and CPO architectures, with independent CW capacity coming online via Win Semi during a structural bottleneck. As a description of where the company sits in [[photonics]], that is fair and it is genuinely high-beta exposure to the CW laser squeeze.

The other two supports do not survive checking.

He argues the CEO is aligned because he buys stock on the open market. The CEO did buy **70,000 shares**. But on **16 July 2026**, the day a lock-up from the April directed issue expired, the Chairman sold **275,000 shares** and board member Todd Thomson sold **950,000 shares** through Headwaters Capital. The two most senior board figures sold roughly 1.2 million shares in the same window in which the CEO bought seventy thousand. That is a split signal, not alignment.

He also credits "low dilution to get all of this done". The company issued **12,280,701 new shares at SEK 57** on 1 July, raising approximately **SEK 700M** — upsized from an indicated SEK 600M — and separately converted roughly **SEK 109M** of debt into equity. Whatever else that is, it is not low dilution.

Underneath the narrative, Q1 revenue fell **22%** year on year to **SEK 61.9M**, the company has pre-announced revenue expected in H1 slipping into H2, and Q2 carries a **SEK 42.9M** non-cash social-security charge. Q2 lands on **27 August**.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
The positioning is real. If the CW laser bottleneck is as structural as the rest of this week's evidence suggests, a small supplier with independent capacity coming online is the highest-torque way to own it, and the SemiNex and CPO development programmes point the right direction.

The Nasdaq listing ambition, if it lands, widens the buyer base considerably.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The desk has no numbers for a print that is six days away, after an extraordinary twelve-month move and a pre-announced revenue slip. That is a position-sizing problem before it is a conviction problem.

The SemiNex programme he cites is a **$3.4M development contract** targeting early production in H2 2027 — a qualification milestone, not capacity, and it changes no shipped volume in 2026 or 2027.

And the analyst holds this personally and says so. That is honest of him, and it is exactly when a second opinion has to check the load-bearing claims rather than the conclusion.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Wait until 27 August. Do not average down the existing dip-buy into the print. After the numbers, the test is simple: did the slipped H1 revenue actually land in H2.

memos.title: Read the margin line first
memos.dek: $NVDA stays at wait into the 26 August print. The number that matters for this whole book is gross margin, not revenue.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: NVIDIA reports fiscal Q2 2027 on **26 August**. Every verdict in this book is written ahead of it. The stance does not move five days before a print.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
His framing this week is that NVIDIA telegraphs each theme roughly a year early and the market dismisses it every time — EML and laser capacity in 2025, then CW capacity, the 800V shift, explicit CPO commitments and physical AI in 2026. On the record of the last cycle that argument has earned its keep, and it is the reason this desk's map is shaped the way it is.

For the print itself, the useful number is not the headline. NVIDIA has guided fiscal Q2 to **$91.0B plus or minus 2%**, two quarters after delivering $81.6B, with GAAP gross margin guided at **74.9%**.

That margin line is the supply-chain signal. Guiding 74.9% while HBM, ABF substrate and advanced-packaging costs are all inflating means NVIDIA expects to **absorb its own suppliers' cost increases rather than pass them through**. If it holds, the pricing power this desk has been tracking across [[memory]] and [[photonics]] is real and NVIDIA is paying for it — which validates the supplier names. If it slips, the entire read-through gets repriced in one line.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: It remains the demand hub the whole map hangs from, and the forward commitments it keeps making are the leading indicator that has worked repeatedly.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
A $91B guide two quarters after $81.6B leaves no room for a supply-driven shortfall to be read as anything other than demand weakness. Holding into the print is a bet on the guide holding, which is a different risk from the buildout thesis and should be sized as such.

The concentration risk is not NVIDIA's alone: a disappointing margin line repricess $LITE, $COHR, $AAOI, $MU and the rest of this book simultaneously. This is the one event where the desk's diversification is largely illusory.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Wait. No action before 26 August. Read gross margin first, revenue second, and let every supplier-name sizing decision in this book wait for it rather than anticipate it.

memos.title: The boring way to own the demand side
memos.dek: $AMZN enters coverage at accumulate. He keeps pointing at the suppliers; this is the risk-adjusted way to own the same spending.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Amazon enters written coverage at accumulate, having carried the stance without a memo. It is the desk's primary [[hyperscalers]] exposure alongside $GOOGL.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
He names AWS and the Trainium ramp repeatedly, but each time says the position he actually wants is the supplier — Alchip, not Amazon. That is a fair read of where the operating leverage is, and a poor read of where the risk-adjusted return is.

Q2 net sales were **$200.6B, up 20%**, with AWS up **37%** — its fastest growth in eighteen quarters — at a **$169B annualised run-rate** and **$16.6B** of segment operating income. Property and equipment purchases rose **$66.1B** year on year on AI.

One caveat specific to this desk's map: AWS capacity at this growth rate is increasingly gated by power and datacenter shell availability rather than by silicon, which makes the [[power]] layer a tighter read on AWS's 2027 ceiling than the accelerator layer is.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body:
It is the lowest-variance way to own the demand side of this map. The suppliers offer more torque and considerably more single-technology risk; Amazon offers the spending itself, funded by a business that already works.

The Trainium programme also means Amazon captures some of the silicon economics it would otherwise pay away.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow has swung to a **$7.6B outflow** on that capital spending. Amazon is funding this build from its own balance sheet, so the equity question has moved from whether AWS grows to whether the depreciation is ever earned back.

That is the same question sitting under every hyperscaler, and it is not answerable from a single quarter. It is answerable from the trend: growth decelerating while capex stays high is the pattern that would break it.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Accumulate on weakness, in tranches rather than at once. Core-sized and held for years. The stance goes to wait on two consecutive quarters of AWS growth below 30% with capex unchanged.

memos.title: Ranked eighth, argued zero times
memos.dek: $TSLA enters coverage at pass — as the standing example of why rank is not importance in this book.

sections.heading: Snapshot
sections.body: Tesla sits eighth by priority score and has no position, no thesis and no desk conviction. It gets a memo precisely because that combination is confusing on the surface, and the explanation is worth writing down once.

sections.heading: Thesis
sections.body:
Of the twenty-one times the analyst has argued Tesla, seventeen are neutral. This week he named it three times and made no investment case in any of them.

He noted that Optimus's form factor should converge toward a human shape. He observed that Optimus is wrapped inside a company worth over a trillion dollars, and therefore is **not** the pure-play humanoid exposure he is pointing at — he was pointing at $CCXI and Unitree. And on general-purpose robotics he said plainly that he does not think Tesla can pull it off yet.

That is three mentions and zero arguments. The priority score cannot tell the difference, because it measures how often a symbol appears in his posts, and large-cap names appear constantly inside multi-ticker recap posts without any conviction attached.

sections.heading: Why own it
sections.body: Nothing in this file supports owning it. If Optimus ever produces a dated, quantified production or revenue commitment that he argues rather than relays, this becomes a real name in this book.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body:
The risk being managed here is the desk's own, not Tesla's: mistaking rank for importance. Tiering is mention-driven, which means a name that gets name-dropped in recap posts can rank top-ten on no conviction, while a genuinely load-bearing name the analyst never mentions cannot rise above radar however important it is.

Tesla is the clearest live example of the first failure mode. The [[power]] layer names are the clearest example of the second.

sections.heading: Bottom line
sections.body: Pass, no position. Kept on the roster as the running check on the scoring model — if Tesla ever leaves the top ten without having been argued once, the score is working.
